wrong_reasons.B: putting both policies on one group gives everyone AdministratorAccess, so nothing changes.
wrong_reasons.C: attaching policies to each user one by one is harder to manage, and the tag does nothing.
wrong_reasons.D: inline policies per user are the hardest to manage, and the tag does nothing.

question: An online marketplace uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB) as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Amazon EC2 instances behind the ALB serve the application. Sellers upload product images to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company recently expanded internationally and needs to dynamically add AWS Region-specific compliance watermarks to images based on the location of the viewer. The solution must not store separate copies for each Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Changing image content at request time needs code at the edge. Policies only manage headers.

options.A: Deploy image processing software on the EC2 instances to add watermarks based on the viewer's location.
options.B: Create a CloudFront origin request policy to add watermarks based on the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header.
options.C: Use a Lambda@Edge function that uses an image processing library associated with the CloudFront cache behavior for images.
options.D: Create a CloudFront response headers policy to add watermarks based on the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header.

explanation: A is wrong: processing on the EC2 fleet adds load and work to the origin for every image.
B is wrong: an origin request policy only chooses which headers reach the origin; it cannot change images.
C is correct: Lambda@Edge can read the viewer's country and add the right watermark as the image is served, so no per-Region copies are stored.
D is wrong: a response headers policy only adds or removes headers; it cannot change image content.
tldr: Changing content per viewer at the edge (watermarks, resizing) needs Lambda@Edge; CloudFront policies only handle headers.

wrong_reasons.A: processing on the EC2 fleet adds load and work to the origin for every image.
wrong_reasons.B: an origin request policy only chooses which headers reach the origin; it cannot change images.
wrong_reasons.D: a response headers policy only adds or removes headers; it cannot change image content.

question: A company uses an organization in AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts. Multiple teams access each AWS account by assuming IAM roles. Each team has a unique IAM role. Each IAM role has a unique set of permissions. A security team wants to automate some security tasks by deploying AWS Lambda functions within each AWS account. The security team wants to ensure that only members of the security team can modify the Lambda functions directly. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: SCPs have no Principal element for naming who is exempt. How do you exclude one role from a deny statement?
keywords: only members of the security team can modify the Lambda functions

options.A: Create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any entity from making changes to Lambda functions except for the IAM role of the security team that is specified in the Principal key. Attach the SCP to the root of the organization.
options.B: Create an IAM policy that denies all changes to the Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) of the Lambda functions. Attach the IAM policy to the root user of each AWS account.
options.C: Create a service control policy (SCP) that denies all changes to Lambda functions. Attach the SCP to the root of the organization.
options.D: Create a service control policy (SCP) that prevents any entity from making changes to Lambda functions except for the IAM role of the security team that is specified in the Condition clause. Attach the SCP to the root of the organization.

explanation: A is wrong: SCPs do not support a Principal element for choosing who is affected.
B is wrong: IAM policies cannot be attached to the root user, and this would not allow the security team either.
C is wrong: denying all changes also blocks the security team.
D is correct: an SCP that denies Lambda changes unless aws:PrincipalArn matches the security team's role lets only that team modify the functions in every account.
tldr: To exempt a role from an SCP deny, use a Condition such as aws:PrincipalArn; SCPs do not support naming principals.

wrong_reasons.A: SCPs do not support a Principal element for choosing who is affected.
wrong_reasons.B: IAM policies cannot be attached to the root user, and this would not allow the security team either.
wrong_reasons.C: denying all changes also blocks the security team.

question: A company wants to build a serverless application in which multiple microservices need to exchange messages. The company needs to ensure that messages that the microservices send to one another are processed exactly once in the exact order the messages are sent. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
hint: Exactly once and in order: which queue type guarantees both?

options.A: Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Configure the microservices to use the SQS queue to exchange messages.
options.B: Use Amazon SNS topics to connect the microservices to one another. Subscribe the microservices to the SNS topics. Use the Amazon SNS API to send and receive notifications between microservices.
options.C: Create an Amazon SQS standard queue. Connect the microservices to one another by using Amazon EventBridge events that the microservices exchange through the SQS queue.
options.D: Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) on Amazon EC2 instances to deploy the application.

explanation: A is correct: a FIFO queue keeps messages in the order they were sent and removes duplicates, so each is processed exactly once, and it is fully managed.
B is wrong: SNS standard topics do not guarantee order or exactly-once delivery, and SNS is not used to receive messages.
C is wrong: a standard queue can deliver out of order and more than once, and adding EventBridge makes it more complex.
D is wrong: self-managing Kafka on EC2 is heavy operational work.
tldr: SQS FIFO queues give ordered, exactly-once processing with no servers to run.

wrong_reasons.B: SNS standard topics do not guarantee order or exactly-once delivery, and SNS is not used to receive messages.
wrong_reasons.C: a standard queue can deliver out of order and more than once, and adding EventBridge makes it more complex.
wrong_reasons.D: self-managing Kafka on EC2 is heavy operational work.

question: A company stores data across 200 Amazon S3 buckets that multiple departments use. Each department has prefix-based tenant isolation for each team in the department. The finance team needs to identify which specific buckets and prefixes are driving the highest S3 costs. The finance team needs bucket-level and prefix-level storage usage and request patterns and the dollar costs attributed to each bucket. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: One tool shows usage and activity down to the prefix; another shows the dollar cost of each bucket.
keywords: bucket-level and prefix-level storage usage and request patterns
dollar costs attributed to each bucket

options.A: Enable S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics. Activate prefix-level aggregation to view storage usage and request activity for each bucket and each prefix.
options.B: Use the S3 Storage Lens free tier to view storage usage. Configure S3 server access logging to view request patterns.
options.C: Configure AWS Cost and Usage Reports to use resource-level granularity to identify costs for each bucket by usage type.
options.D: Use AWS Cost Explorer. Apply cost allocation tags to view S3 costs grouped by bucket and usage type.
options.E: Enable S3 server access logging on all buckets. Query the logs by using Amazon Athena to calculate costs for each prefix.

explanation: A is correct: Storage Lens advanced metrics with prefix aggregation show storage and request activity for every bucket and prefix.
B is wrong: the free tier has no prefix-level or activity metrics, and access logs must be processed before they are useful.
C is correct: the Cost and Usage Report with resource IDs lists the cost of each bucket by usage type.
D is wrong: cost allocation tags would have to be applied to all 200 buckets first, and they still do not show prefixes.
E is wrong: access logs show requests, not dollar costs, and turning them into costs is custom work.
tldr: S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics show usage and requests per bucket and prefix; CUR with resource IDs shows the dollar cost per bucket.

wrong_reasons.B: the free tier has no prefix-level or activity metrics, and access logs must be processed before they are useful.
wrong_reasons.D: cost allocation tags would have to be applied to all 200 buckets first, and they still do not show prefixes.
wrong_reasons.E: access logs show requests, not dollar costs, and turning them into costs is custom work.

question: A company is migrating an application to the AWS Cloud. The application runs in an on-premises data center and writes thousands of images into a mounted NFS file system each night. After the company migrates the application, the company will host the application on an Amazon EC2 instance with a mounted Amazon EFS file system. The company has established an AWS Direct Connect connection to AWS. Before the migration cutover, a solutions architect must build a process that will replicate the newly created on-premises images to the EFS file system. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to replicate the images?
hint: Which service copies directly from on-premises NFS to EFS on a schedule, without S3 in the middle?

options.A: Configure a periodic process to run the aws s3 sync command from the on-premises file system to Amazon S3. Configure an AWS Lambda function to process event notifications from Amazon S3 and copy the images from Amazon S3 to the EFS file system.
options.B: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway with an NFS mount point. Mount the file gateway file system on the on-premises server. Configure a process to periodically copy the images to the mount point.
options.C: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent to an on-premises server that has access to the NFS file system. Send data over the Direct Connect connection to an S3 bucket by using a public VIF. Configure an AWS Lambda function to process event notifications from Amazon S3 and copy the images from Amazon S3 to the EFS file system.
options.D: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent to an on-premises server that has access to the NFS file system. Send data over the Direct Connect connection to an AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EFS by using a private VIF. Configure a DataSync scheduled task to send the images to the EFS file system every 24 hours.

explanation: A is wrong: going through S3 and a Lambda copier adds extra steps and code.
B is wrong: File Gateway writes to S3, not EFS, and the copy process is still manual.
C is wrong: staging in S3 and copying with Lambda adds steps, and a public VIF uses public endpoints.
D is correct: a DataSync agent copies new images directly into EFS on a schedule, privately over Direct Connect, and handles verification and retries.
tldr: DataSync copies from on-premises NFS straight to EFS on a schedule, privately over Direct Connect.

wrong_reasons.A: going through S3 and a Lambda copier adds extra steps and code.
wrong_reasons.B: File Gateway writes to S3, not EFS, and the copy process is still manual.
wrong_reasons.C: staging in S3 and copying with Lambda adds steps, and a public VIF uses public endpoints.

question: A company is building an e-commerce platform that will allow customers to place orders online. Customer traffic varies significantly. An order-processing microservice is running on a group of Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect must ensure that the application remains responsive and decoupled from the frontend. The application must also be able to reprocess orders that the application fails to process on the first attempt. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: What sits between the frontend and the workers, and redelivers a message if processing fails?
keywords: reprocess orders that the application fails to process

options.A: Deploy an Application Load Balancer in front of the order processing microservice. Configure the Amazon EC2 instances to scale out automatically based on CPU utilization metrics as traffic increases.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon SQS queue to integrate the frontend and the order-processing microservice. Configure the frontend to send messages to the queue. Configure the EC2 instances to process messages from the queue.
options.C: Establish direct HTTPS connections from the frontend to the microservice. Use a dynamically expanding thread pool to handle concurrency at the microservice layer.
options.D: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest all order requests from the frontend. Configure the Amazon EC2 instances to continuously poll the stream and process orders in near real time.

explanation: A is wrong: an ALB calls the service directly, so it is not decoupled, and failed requests are lost.
B is correct: SQS buffers orders between the frontend and workers, and a message that fails becomes visible again to be reprocessed.
C is wrong: direct HTTPS calls tightly couple the tiers and lose orders that fail.
D is wrong: Kinesis handles ordered streams, but it is more complex, and per-message retry is not built in the way it is with SQS.
tldr: An SQS queue decouples the frontend from workers; failed messages become visible again and are retried.

wrong_reasons.A: an ALB calls the service directly, so it is not decoupled, and failed requests are lost.
wrong_reasons.C: direct HTTPS calls tightly couple the tiers and lose orders that fail.
wrong_reasons.D: Kinesis handles ordered streams, but it is more complex, and per-message retry is not built in the way it is with SQS.

question: A company is running a critical workload on an Amazon RDS DB instance. The company needs the DB instance to be highly available. The company requires a recovery time of less than 5 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which RDS feature keeps a synchronous standby and fails over automatically?

options.A: Create a read replica of the DB instance.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation to create a template of the DB instance.
options.C: Take periodic snapshots of the DB instance. Store the snapshots in Amazon S3.
options.D: Modify the DB instance to use a Multi-AZ deployment.

explanation: A is wrong: a read replica must be promoted by hand, and replication is asynchronous.
B is wrong: a CloudFormation template recreates infrastructure, not the data, and takes far longer than 5 minutes.
C is wrong: restoring from a snapshot takes too long and loses recent data.
D is correct: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically, usually in 1-2 minutes.
tldr: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby and fails over automatically, typically within 1-2 minutes.

wrong_reasons.A: a read replica must be promoted by hand, and replication is asynchronous.
wrong_reasons.B: a CloudFormation template recreates infrastructure, not the data, and takes far longer than 5 minutes.
wrong_reasons.C: restoring from a snapshot takes too long and loses recent data.

question: A company runs a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) application that stores customer analytics data across two AWS Regions. The company encrypts data at rest and does not want to manage key material directly. The company needs encryption keys that work in both Regions and needs to control key access based on customer tenant identifiers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: You need the same key usable in two Regions, and access based on tags.
keywords: does not want to manage key material

options.A: Use AWS KMS to create multi-Region keys. Apply tags to identify tenant associations for each key. Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) condition keys to control access to the keys.
options.B: Generate key material externally and import the material into separate AWS KMS keys in each Region. Apply tags to identify tenant associations. Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) condition keys to control access.
options.C: Use AWS CloudHSM to create an HSM cluster in the first Region. Copy cluster backups to the second Region and create a new cluster from the backup. Synchronize keys manually by using the CloudHSM CLI.
options.D: Use AWS CloudHSM to provision HSM clusters in both Regions. Create HSM users for each tenant. Use the CloudHSM Management Utility to replicate keys and share them with users in each Region.

explanation: A is correct: multi-Region keys work interchangeably in both Regions with AWS-managed key material, and ABAC on tenant tags controls who can use each key.
B is wrong: importing external key material means generating and protecting it yourself, which the company wants to avoid.
C is wrong: CloudHSM clusters and manual key synchronization are a lot of operational work.
D is wrong: CloudHSM users per tenant and manual key replication are complex to run.
tldr: KMS multi-Region keys share key material across Regions; tag the keys and use ABAC conditions to control access per tenant.

wrong_reasons.B: importing external key material means generating and protecting it yourself, which the company wants to avoid.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudHSM clusters and manual key synchronization are a lot of operational work.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudHSM users per tenant and manual key replication are complex to run.

question: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to serve content to users. The company uses Amazon EBS volumes to store data. The company needs to encrypt data in transit and at rest. Which combination of services will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: One service issues TLS certificates for the ALB; the other manages the keys that encrypt EBS volumes.
keywords: encrypt data in transit and at rest

options.A: Amazon GuardDuty.
options.B: AWS Shield.
options.C: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
options.D: AWS Secrets Manager.
options.E: AWS KMS.

explanation: A is wrong: GuardDuty detects threats; it does not encrypt anything.
B is wrong: Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not encrypt anything.
C is correct: ACM provides the TLS certificates that let the ALB serve HTTPS, which encrypts data in transit.
D is wrong: Secrets Manager stores credentials; it does not encrypt traffic or volumes.
E is correct: KMS manages the keys used to encrypt EBS volumes at rest.
tldr: In transit: ACM certificates on the ALB (HTTPS). At rest: KMS keys for EBS encryption.

wrong_reasons.A: GuardDuty detects threats; it does not encrypt anything.
wrong_reasons.B: Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not encrypt anything.
wrong_reasons.D: Secrets Manager stores credentials; it does not encrypt traffic or volumes.

question: A company is building a serverless application to process large volumes of sensor data. The application uses an AWS Lambda function and stores data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The application needs to handle unpredictable traffic patterns with occasional spikes in data ingestion. The company wants to optimize application performance to respond to spikes in demand. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: One setting keeps Lambda ready for bursts, and one DynamoDB mode absorbs unpredictable traffic without planning capacity.

options.A: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function. Use on-demand capacity mode for the DynamoDB table.
options.B: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function. Use provisioned capacity mode for the DynamoDB table.
options.C: Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda function. Use on-demand capacity mode for the DynamoDB table.
options.D: Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda function. Use provisioned capacity mode for the DynamoDB table.

explanation: A is correct: provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm for bursts, and on-demand mode lets DynamoDB absorb unpredictable spikes without throttling.
B is wrong: provisioned capacity mode must be planned in advance and can throttle during sudden spikes.
C is wrong: reserved concurrency caps and reserves capacity; it does not pre-warm environments.
D is wrong: reserved concurrency does not remove cold starts, and provisioned capacity can throttle during spikes.
tldr: Spiky serverless ingestion: Lambda provisioned concurrency for ready capacity, DynamoDB on-demand for unpredictable throughput.

wrong_reasons.B: provisioned capacity mode must be planned in advance and can throttle during sudden spikes.
wrong_reasons.C: reserved concurrency caps and reserves capacity; it does not pre-warm environments.
wrong_reasons.D: reserved concurrency does not remove cold starts, and provisioned capacity can throttle during spikes.

question: A social media company is expanding its Amazon DynamoDB backed infrastructure to accommodate increasing user activity. The company manages three data types: user profiles, posts, and comments. The company wants to ensure high performance for write-heavy queries. The new solution must ensure high availability. The new solution needs to provide low latency between the database layer and the application layer. The new solution must be able to handle dynamic traffic patterns for global users. The company must also track changes to items in the DynamoDB tables. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Global users and low latency point to multi-Region tables; tracking item changes has a built-in DynamoDB feature.

options.A: Create a single DynamoDB table to store all the data types. Use global secondary indexes (GSIs) for queries. Use DynamoDB auto scaling to ensure adaptive capacity. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to provide low latency and to track changes.
options.B: Use a separate DynamoDB table for each data type. Use on-demand capacity mode for all tables. Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to provide low latency. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to track changes.
options.C: Use DynamoDB global tables to distribute data across AWS Regions and to provide low latency. Use a separate DynamoDB table for each data type. Use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to track changes.
options.D: Create a single DynamoDB table to store all data types. Use provisioned capacity mode to provide low latency. Use composite sort keys for queries. Use Amazon Data Firehose to track changes.

explanation: A is wrong: Kinesis Data Streams does not reduce latency, and a single-Region table does not serve global users well.
B is wrong: DAX speeds up reads, not a write-heavy workload, and a single Region does not serve global users.
C is correct: global tables replicate tables across Regions for low latency and high availability, and DynamoDB Streams records every item change with no extra service.
D is wrong: provisioned capacity does not lower latency, and Firehose delivers data; it does not capture item changes.
tldr: Global, write-heavy DynamoDB: global tables for multi-Region low latency and availability; DynamoDB Streams to track item changes.

wrong_reasons.A: Kinesis Data Streams does not reduce latency, and a single-Region table does not serve global users well.
wrong_reasons.B: DAX speeds up reads, not a write-heavy workload, and a single Region does not serve global users.
wrong_reasons.D: provisioned capacity does not lower latency, and Firehose delivers data; it does not capture item changes.

question: A company uses AWS CloudFormation to provision AWS infrastructure. Multiple application teams create similar networking resources for their workloads. The teams currently copy and modify sections of CloudFormation templates, which causes inconsistent resource configurations across applications. The company needs to provide a reusable standard pattern that the teams can consume. Updates to the pattern must be managed from a central location. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which CloudFormation feature packages resources so templates can reuse them, updated in one place?

options.A: Create reusable CloudFormation modules that define the approved networking patterns. Instruct the teams to use the modules in their templates.
options.B: Create a central repository that contains approved CloudFormation template snippets. Require the teams to copy the relevant snippets into their templates.
options.C: Store a shared CloudFormation template in an Amazon S3 bucket. Instruct each team to copy the most recent version before provisioning resources.
options.D: Create an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook that provisions the approved networking resources for each team.

explanation: A is correct: modules package the approved networking resources as a reusable building block that templates include, and updates are made in one place.
B is wrong: copying snippets is what caused the inconsistency in the first place.
C is wrong: teams copying a shared template still end up with diverging copies.
D is wrong: an Automation runbook bypasses the teams' CloudFormation stacks, so the resources are not part of their templates.
tldr: CloudFormation modules package standard resource configurations for reuse across templates, managed centrally.

wrong_reasons.B: copying snippets is what caused the inconsistency in the first place.
wrong_reasons.C: teams copying a shared template still end up with diverging copies.
wrong_reasons.D: an Automation runbook bypasses the teams' CloudFormation stacks, so the resources are not part of their templates.

question: A company wants to design a microservices architecture for an application. Each microservice must perform operations that can be completed within 30 seconds. The microservices need to expose RESTful APIs and must automatically scale in response to varying loads. The APIs must also provide client access control and rate limiting to maintain equitable usage and service availability. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Short operations, automatic scaling, and an API front door with throttling and API keys.
keywords: client access control and rate limiting

options.A: Use Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2 to host each microservice. Use Amazon API Gateway to manage the RESTful API requests.
options.B: Deploy each microservice as a set of AWS Lambda functions. Use Amazon API Gateway to manage the RESTful API requests.
options.C: Host each microservice on Amazon EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups behind an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer. Use the ELB to manage the RESTful API requests.
options.D: Deploy each microservice on Amazon Elastic Beanstalk. Use Amazon CloudFront to manage the RESTful API requests.

explanation: A is wrong: ECS on EC2 means managing and scaling a cluster of instances.
B is correct: Lambda scales automatically and fits 30-second operations, and API Gateway provides authorization, throttling and usage plans.
C is wrong: EC2 fleets need management, and a load balancer has no API keys or per-client rate limiting.
D is wrong: CloudFront is a CDN; it does not provide API access control or usage plans.
tldr: Lambda behind API Gateway gives auto-scaling REST APIs with built-in authorization, throttling and usage plans.

wrong_reasons.A: ECS on EC2 means managing and scaling a cluster of instances.
wrong_reasons.C: EC2 fleets need management, and a load balancer has no API keys or per-client rate limiting.
wrong_reasons.D: CloudFront is a CDN; it does not provide API access control or usage plans.

question: A healthcare company receives de-identified medical records from hospital partners that upload data to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket. A regulatory agency requires encryption of all stored health information. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Encryption at rest is requested with a specific header on each PUT. Which condition checks for it?
keywords: encryption of all stored health information

options.A: Configure a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests when the s3:x-amz-acl condition key is not present in the request headers.
options.B: Configure a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests when the s3:x-amz-acl condition key is not set to bucket-owner-full-control in the request.
options.C: Configure a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests when the aws:SecureTransport condition key is not set to true in the request.
options.D: Configure a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests when the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption header is not present in the request.

explanation: A is wrong: x-amz-acl sets object ACLs; it has nothing to do with encryption.
B is wrong: bucket-owner-full-control is about object ownership, not encryption.
C is wrong: aws:SecureTransport enforces encryption in transit, not at rest.
D is correct: denying any PutObject without the server-side encryption header ensures every stored object is encrypted at rest.
tldr: A bucket policy can deny PutObject requests without the x-amz-server-side-encryption header (S3 also encrypts new objects with SSE-S3 by default).

wrong_reasons.A: x-amz-acl sets object ACLs; it has nothing to do with encryption.
wrong_reasons.B: bucket-owner-full-control is about object ownership, not encryption.
wrong_reasons.C: aws:SecureTransport enforces encryption in transit, not at rest.

question: A company provides a three-tier web application to its customers. Each customer has an AWS account in which the application is deployed, and These accounts are members of the company's organization in AWS Organizations. To protect its customers' AWS accounts and applications, the company wants to monitor them for unusual and unexpected behavior. The company needs to analyze and monitor customer VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail logs, and DNS logs. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?
hint: Which service analyzes exactly these three log sources for threats, with a delegated administrator for the organization?
keywords: VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail logs, and DNS logs

options.A: Designate an account in the organization as the AWS Shield administrator account. Enable Shield and Shield logs in every account, and invite the accounts to join the Shield administrator account. Analyze Shield findings in the Shield administrator account.
options.B: Designate an account in the organization as the Amazon GuardDuty administrator account. Enable GuardDuty in every account, and invite the accounts to join the GuardDuty administrator account. Analyze GuardDuty findings in the GuardDuty administrator account.
options.C: Designate an account in the organization as the AWS WAF administrator account. Enable AWS WAF and AWS WAF logs in every account, and invite the accounts to join the AWS WAF administrator account. Analyze AWS WAF logs in the AWS WAF administrator account.
options.D: Designate an account in the organization as the AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) administrator account. Enable AWS RAM in every account, and invite the accounts to join the AWS RAM administrator account. Analyze AWS RAM logs in the AWS RAM administrator account.

explanation: A is wrong: Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not analyze these logs for unusual behavior.
B is correct: GuardDuty analyzes VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail and DNS logs for threats, and an administrator account collects findings from every member account.
C is wrong: WAF filters web requests; it does not analyze flow, CloudTrail or DNS logs.
D is wrong: Resource Access Manager shares resources between accounts; it does not monitor anything.
tldr: GuardDuty analyzes VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail and DNS logs for threats; a delegated administrator account centralizes findings.

wrong_reasons.A: Shield protects against DDoS attacks; it does not analyze these logs for unusual behavior.
wrong_reasons.C: WAF filters web requests; it does not analyze flow, CloudTrail or DNS logs.
wrong_reasons.D: Resource Access Manager shares resources between accounts; it does not monitor anything.

question: A company needs to use container images for a new project. A development team requires full access to a new Amazon ECR repository. A solutions architect creates a new IAM role that has the AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryFullAccess policy attached. The solutions architect creates a second ECR repository by using an existing repository as a template. When a developer tries to push a docker image to the second repository by using the new IAM role, the command fails with an authorization error. What is the likely cause of the error?
hint: The role has full ECR permissions. What could still deny the push, and what did the template copy?
keywords: using an existing repository as a template

options.A: The token that the developer retrieved to log in to the docker repository by using the aws ecr get-login-password command is older than 2 hours.
options.B: The IAM role that is assigned to the development team does not have permission to pull images from the repository.
options.C: The developer does not have multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled.
options.D: The new repository was created from an ECR repository policy that denies pushing images.

explanation: A is wrong: the token from get-login-password is valid for 12 hours, so a 2-hour-old token is still valid.
B is wrong: pulling is not what failed, and the full-access policy includes pull permissions anyway.
C is wrong: the ECR full-access policy does not require MFA.
D is correct: the new repository copied a repository policy that denies pushes, and an explicit Deny overrides the role's IAM Allow.
tldr: An explicit Deny in a resource policy overrides IAM Allows; a repository created from a template can inherit a repository policy that denies pushes.

wrong_reasons.A: the token from get-login-password is valid for 12 hours, so a 2-hour-old token is still valid.
wrong_reasons.B: pulling is not what failed, and the full-access policy includes pull permissions anyway.
wrong_reasons.C: the ECR full-access policy does not require MFA.

question: A company stores image files in an Amazon S3 bucket in one AWS Region. Development teams in multiple AWS accounts that the company owns need to pull the image files repeatedly for their application deployments, from pipelines that run in other AWS Regions and in on-premises data centers. The company wants to provide access to the image files while reducing costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Many teams pull the same files again and again. What serves repeated downloads from a cache instead of from S3 each time?
keywords: other AWS Regions and in on-premises data centers

options.A: Configure an interface VPC endpoint for the bucket.
options.B: Use the Requester Pays configuration on the bucket.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution to deliver the image files.
options.D: Configure the bucket to allow access only through AWS PrivateLink endpoints.

explanation: A is wrong: an interface endpoint adds hourly and per-GB charges, and it only gives private network access; it does not reduce the number of downloads or their cost.
B is wrong: Requester Pays only moves the request and transfer charges to the teams' own accounts. The company owns those accounts, so its total cost does not go down.

C is correct: the pulls come from other Regions and from on premises, so every direct download from S3 is charged as data transfer out. CloudFront serves repeated pulls from its cache, transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront data transfer out costs less than transfer out directly from S3.
D is wrong: PrivateLink-only access adds endpoint charges and does not reduce the cost of repeated downloads.
tldr: For repeated downloads from outside the bucket's Region, CloudFront cuts cost: S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and cached pulls skip S3 entirely.

wrong_reasons.A: an interface endpoint adds hourly and per-GB charges, and it only gives private network access; it does not reduce the number of downloads or their cost.
wrong_reasons.B: Requester Pays only moves the request and transfer charges to the teams' own accounts. The company owns those accounts, so its total cost does not go down.
wrong_reasons.D: PrivateLink-only access adds endpoint charges and does not reduce the cost of repeated downloads.

question: A solutions architect is managing an application in the us-west-1 Region and wants to set up disaster recovery in the us-east-1 Region. The Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster needs RPO of 1 minute and an RTO of 2 minutes. Which approach meets these requirements with no negative performance impact?
hint: Which Aurora feature replicates to another Region at the storage layer, usually in under a second?
keywords: RPO of 1 minute and an RTO of 2 minutes

options.A: Enable synchronous replication.
options.B: Enable asynchronous binlog replication.
options.C: Create an Aurora Global Database.
options.D: Copy Aurora incremental snapshots to the us-east-1 Region.

explanation: A is wrong: synchronous replication across Regions would add latency to every write.
B is wrong: binlog replication adds load on the primary and is slower to fail over.
C is correct: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typically under 1 second of lag and can promote the secondary in about a minute, without slowing the primary.
D is wrong: copying snapshots gives an RPO of hours and a long restore.
tldr: Aurora Global Database replicates across Regions in about a second (RPO) and promotes a secondary in about a minute (RTO).

wrong_reasons.A: synchronous replication across Regions would add latency to every write.
wrong_reasons.B: binlog replication adds load on the primary and is slower to fail over.
wrong_reasons.D: copying snapshots gives an RPO of hours and a long restore.

question: A company runs several Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The company needs to be able to copy files directly to the EC2 instances. The company wants to use standard Linux tools such as secure copy protocol (SCP) or SFTP. Security controls prohibit inbound SSH access or public IP address assignment to any EC2 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements while following AWS security best practices?
hint: Which option needs no inbound port at all, yet can carry an SSH session for SCP?
keywords: prohibit inbound SSH access or public IP address

options.A: Use an Amazon S3 bucket for file transfer. Configure the EC2 instances to download files from Amazon S3 on demand.
options.B: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint. Use the EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint to establish a session for file transfer.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with an instance profile and the local plugin.
options.D: Use AWS Transfer Family with an SFTP endpoint connected to the private VPC for managed file transfers.

explanation: A is wrong: downloading from S3 is not copying directly to the instances with SCP or SFTP.
B is wrong: an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint still needs the instances' security groups to allow inbound SSH from the endpoint, which the controls prohibit.
C is correct: Session Manager, with the local plugin and an SSH ProxyCommand, carries SCP and SFTP through the agent's outbound connection, so no inbound port or public IP is needed.
D is wrong: Transfer Family stores files in S3 or EFS, not directly on the EC2 instances.
tldr: SSH over Session Manager lets SCP and SFTP work with no inbound ports or public IPs; the SSM agent makes an outbound connection.

wrong_reasons.A: downloading from S3 is not copying directly to the instances with SCP or SFTP.
wrong_reasons.B: an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint still needs the instances' security groups to allow inbound SSH from the endpoint, which the controls prohibit.
wrong_reasons.D: Transfer Family stores files in S3 or EFS, not directly on the EC2 instances.

question: A company is building a solution to provide customers with an API that accesses financial data. The API backend needs to compute tax data for each request. The company anticipates greater demand to access the data during the last 3 months of each year. A solutions architect needs to design a scalable solution that can meet the regular demand and the peak demand at the end of each year. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Demand swings with the season. Which option scales automatically in both directions without managing servers?
keywords: compute tax data for each request
regular demand and the peak demand

options.A: Host the API on an Amazon EC2 instance that runs third-party software. Configure the EC2 instance to perform tax computations.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Create an AWS Lambda function to perform tax computations. Integrate the Lambda function with the REST API.
options.C: Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of two Amazon EC2 instances. Configure the EC2 instances to perform tax computations.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Configure an Amazon EC2 instance to perform tax computations. Integrate the EC2 instance with the REST API.

explanation: A is wrong: a single EC2 instance cannot scale for the year-end peak and is a single point of failure.
B is correct: API Gateway and Lambda scale automatically with each request, handle the year-end peak, and cost nothing during quiet periods.
C is wrong: two fixed EC2 instances do not scale out for the peak.
D is wrong: API Gateway scales, but one EC2 instance behind it becomes the bottleneck.
tldr: Seasonal, request-driven APIs suit API Gateway + Lambda: they scale with each request and cost nothing when idle.

wrong_reasons.A: a single EC2 instance cannot scale for the year-end peak and is a single point of failure.
wrong_reasons.C: two fixed EC2 instances do not scale out for the peak.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway scales, but one EC2 instance behind it becomes the bottleneck.

question: A company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts a website both on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company's on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company hosts the website on AWS in the eu-central-1 Region. The company wants to optimize load times for the website as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which Route 53 routing policy sends each user to the location with the lowest latency, including non-AWS locations tied to a Region?
keywords: on premises and in the AWS Cloud

options.A: Create a DNS record with a failover routing policy that routes all primary traffic to eu-central-1. Configure the routing policy to use the on-premises data center as the secondary location.
options.B: Create a DNS record with an IP-based routing policy. Configure specific IP ranges to return the value for the eu-central-1 website. Configure all other IP ranges to return the value for the on-premises website.
options.C: Create a DNS record with a latency-based routing policy. Associate the record for the on-premises data center with us-west-1.
options.D: Create a DNS record with a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.

explanation: A is wrong: failover sends everyone to eu-central-1 unless it fails, so users near us-west-1 get slow loads.
B is wrong: IP-based routing needs you to maintain IP ranges by hand and does not measure latency.
C is correct: latency-based routing sends each user to the faster location, and associating the on-premises record with us-west-1 lets Route 53 estimate its latency.
D is wrong: weighted routing splits traffic regardless of where users are.
tldr: Latency-based routing sends users to the lowest-latency endpoint; associate an on-premises endpoint with its nearest Region.

wrong_reasons.A: failover sends everyone to eu-central-1 unless it fails, so users near us-west-1 get slow loads.
wrong_reasons.B: IP-based routing needs you to maintain IP ranges by hand and does not measure latency.
wrong_reasons.D: weighted routing splits traffic regardless of where users are.

question: A company is developing a content sharing platform that currently handles 500 GB of user-generated media files. The company expects the amount of content to grow significantly in the future. The company needs a storage solution that can automatically scale, provide high durability, and allow direct user uploads from web browsers. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Unlimited growth, very high durability and browser uploads (for example with presigned URLs).
keywords: direct user uploads from web browsers

options.A: Store the data in an Amazon EBS volume with Multi-Attach enabled.
options.B: Store the data in an Amazon EFS Standard file system.
options.C: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Standard bucket.
options.D: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Express One Zone bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: EBS volumes have a fixed size, live in one Availability Zone and cannot take uploads from browsers.
B is wrong: EFS costs far more per GB and has no browser upload path.
C is correct: S3 Standard scales without limit, stores data across multiple Availability Zones for 11 nines of durability, supports direct browser uploads, and costs the least per GB here.
D is wrong: S3 Express One Zone stores data in a single Availability Zone at a higher price; it is built for low-latency access, not cheap durable storage.
tldr: User media at scale: S3 Standard gives unlimited, highly durable storage with direct browser uploads through presigned URLs.

wrong_reasons.A: EBS volumes have a fixed size, live in one Availability Zone and cannot take uploads from browsers.
wrong_reasons.B: EFS costs far more per GB and has no browser upload path.
wrong_reasons.D: S3 Express One Zone stores data in a single Availability Zone at a higher price; it is built for low-latency access, not cheap durable storage.

question: A company has deployed infrastructure on AWS. A solutions architect wants to create an AWS Lambda function that will retrieve data from an Amazon Aurora database. The Amazon Aurora database is in a private subnet in company's VPC. The VPC is named VPC1. The data is relational in nature. The Lambda function needs to access the data securely. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Lambda must run inside the VPC, and the security group rules must let it reach the database port.

options.A: Create the Lambda function. Configure VPC1 access for the function. Attach a security group named SG1 to both the Lambda function and the database. Configure the security group inbound and outbound rules to allow TCP traffic on Port 3306.
options.B: Create and launch a Lambda function in a new public subnet that is in a new VPC named VPC2. Create a peering connection between VPC1 and VPC2.
options.C: Create the Lambda function. Configure VPC1 access for the function. Assign a security group named SG1 to the Lambda function. Assign a second security group named SG2 to the database. Add an inbound rule to SG1 to allow TCP traffic from Port 3306.
options.D: Export the data from the Aurora database to Amazon S3. Create and launch a Lambda function in VPC1. Configure the Lambda function query the data from Amazon S3.

explanation: A is correct: attaching the function to VPC1 and giving both the function and the database a security group that allows TCP 3306 between its members lets the function reach the database privately.
B is wrong: a public subnet in a new VPC with peering is more complex and less secure than attaching the function to VPC1.
C is wrong: the inbound rule is on the wrong group; the database's group must allow traffic from the function, not the other way round.
D is wrong: exporting relational data to S3 loses the live database and adds a pipeline to maintain.
tldr: VPC-attached Lambda reaches a private database through security group rules: one shared group, or the database group allowing the function's group.

wrong_reasons.B: a public subnet in a new VPC with peering is more complex and less secure than attaching the function to VPC1.
wrong_reasons.C: the inbound rule is on the wrong group; the database's group must allow traffic from the function, not the other way round.
wrong_reasons.D: exporting relational data to S3 loses the live database and adds a pipeline to maintain.

question: A media streaming company needs to deploy its video processing application across multiple Availability Zones for high availability. The application consists of containerized microservices that process video files. The microservices must automatically recover from failures. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Containers across Availability Zones with automatic recovery, and no servers to manage.

options.A: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type.
options.B: Deploy the containers to Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes.
options.C: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type.
options.D: Deploy the containers to Amazon EC2 instances.

explanation: A is wrong: the EC2 launch type means managing and patching the container instances.
B is wrong: EKS with self-managed nodes is the most operational work of the container options.
C is correct: Fargate runs tasks across Availability Zones without servers, and the ECS service replaces failed tasks automatically.
D is wrong: plain EC2 instances have no container orchestration or automatic recovery.
tldr: ECS on Fargate runs containers across AZs and replaces failed tasks automatically, with no instances to manage.

wrong_reasons.A: the EC2 launch type means managing and patching the container instances.
wrong_reasons.B: EKS with self-managed nodes is the most operational work of the container options.
wrong_reasons.D: plain EC2 instances have no container orchestration or automatic recovery.

question: A solutions architect is designing a three-tier web application. The architecture consists of an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a web tier that is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The application tier with the business logic runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. The database tier consists of Microsoft SQL Server that runs on EC2 instances in private subnets. Security is a high priority for the company. Which combination of security group configurations should the solutions architect use? (Select THREE.)
hint: Chain the tiers: each tier accepts traffic only from the tier in front of it, referenced by security group.

options.A: Configure the security group for the web tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the ALB.
options.B: Configure the security group for the web tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
options.C: Configure the security group for the database tier to allow inbound Microsoft SQL Server traffic from the security group for the application tier.
options.D: Configure the security group for the database tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.
options.E: Configure the security group for the application tier to allow inbound HTTPS traffic from the security group for the web tier.
options.F: Configure the security group for the application tier to allow outbound HTTPS traffic and Microsoft SQL Server traffic to the security group for the web tier.

explanation: A is correct: the web tier should accept HTTPS only from the ALB's security group.
B is wrong: opening all outbound HTTPS to the internet is not needed to serve the application and weakens security.
C is correct: the database should accept SQL Server traffic only from the application tier's security group.
D is wrong: the database never starts connections to the web tier, and the web tier should not talk to the database at all.
E is correct: the application tier should accept HTTPS only from the web tier's security group.
F is wrong: the application tier sends SQL traffic to the database, not to the web tier.
tldr: Tiered security groups: web allows the ALB group, app allows the web group, database allows the app group.

wrong_reasons.B: opening all outbound HTTPS to the internet is not needed to serve the application and weakens security.
wrong_reasons.D: the database never starts connections to the web tier, and the web tier should not talk to the database at all.
wrong_reasons.F: the application tier sends SQL traffic to the database, not to the web tier.

question: A company uses AWS Cost Explorer to monitor its AWS costs. The company notices that Amazon EBS storage and snapshot costs increase every month. However, the company does not purchase additional EBS storage every month. The company wants to optimize monthly costs for its current storage usage. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Snapshots are piling up. What removes the unneeded ones and keeps new ones under a retention policy automatically?
keywords: does not purchase additional EBS storage

options.A: Use logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor the storage utilization of Amazon EBS. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
options.B: Use a custom script to monitor space usage. Use Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes to reduce the size of the EBS volumes.
options.C: Delete all expired and unused snapshots to reduce snapshot costs.
options.D: Delete all nonessential snapshots. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create and manage the snapshots according to the company's snapshot policy requirements.

explanation: A is wrong: the storage is not growing, so shrinking volumes does not address snapshot growth, and EBS volumes cannot be made smaller in place.
B is wrong: a custom script adds work, and EBS volumes cannot be shrunk with Elastic Volumes.
C is wrong: a one-time cleanup helps, but snapshots will pile up again without a retention policy.
D is correct: deleting nonessential snapshots cuts today's cost, and Data Lifecycle Manager creates and expires snapshots by policy so the cost stops growing.
tldr: Growing EBS snapshot costs: delete the unneeded snapshots, then let Data Lifecycle Manager create and expire them by policy.

wrong_reasons.A: the storage is not growing, so shrinking volumes does not address snapshot growth, and EBS volumes cannot be made smaller in place.
wrong_reasons.B: a custom script adds work, and EBS volumes cannot be shrunk with Elastic Volumes.
wrong_reasons.C: a one-time cleanup helps, but snapshots will pile up again without a retention policy.

question: A company wants to optimize costs for an Amazon EC2 instance that has an attached Amazon EBS volume. The EC2 instance provides compute resources for an application that is often unused for scheduled periods of up to 30 days. The application requires the EC2 instance to retain its private IPv4 address. Additionally, the contents of the instance's RAM must be retained. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Keeping RAM contents across a stop is exactly one EC2 feature.
keywords: unused for scheduled periods of up to 30 days
contents of the instance's RAM must be retained

options.A: Create a daily Amazon Machine Image (AMI) snapshot backup of the EC2 instance. Terminate the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. Create a new EC2 instance from the most recent AMI backup when needed.
options.B: Ensure that hibernation mode is enabled on the EC2 instance. Transition the EC2 instance into hibernation mode during periods when the application is not required. Restart the EC2 instance when needed.
options.C: Create hourly backups of the EBS volume by using Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager. Terminate the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. When the application is required, create a new EC2 instance and restore the EBS volume from the most recent backup.
options.D: Ensure that stop protection is disabled on the EC2 instance. Stop the EC2 instance during periods when the application is not required. Restart the EC2 instance when needed.

explanation: A is wrong: a new instance from an AMI gets a new private IP address and loses the RAM contents.
B is correct: hibernation writes RAM to the EBS root volume, keeps the private IP address, and stops compute charges while the instance sleeps.
C is wrong: a new instance loses the private IP address and the RAM contents.
D is wrong: a normal stop keeps the private IP address, but the RAM contents are lost.
tldr: Hibernation saves RAM to the EBS root volume and keeps the private IP, while you pay nothing for the stopped instance's compute.

wrong_reasons.A: a new instance from an AMI gets a new private IP address and loses the RAM contents.
wrong_reasons.C: a new instance loses the private IP address and the RAM contents.
wrong_reasons.D: a normal stop keeps the private IP address, but the RAM contents are lost.

question: A company has a regional subscription-based streaming service that runs in a single AWS Region. The architecture consists of web servers and application servers on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in Auto Scaling groups behind Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancers. The architecture includes an Amazon Aurora global database cluster that extends across multiple Availability Zones. The company wants to expand globally and to ensure that its application has minimal downtime. Which solution will provide the MOST fault tolerance?
hint: Auto Scaling groups cannot span Regions. Which database feature replicates across Regions with fast promotion?

options.A: Extend the Auto Scaling groups for the web tier and the application tier to deploy instances in Availability Zones in a second Region. Use an Aurora global database to deploy the database in the primary Region and the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region.
options.B: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Add an Aurora PostgreSQL cross-Region Aurora Replica in the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region. Promote the secondary to primary as needed.
options.C: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Create an Aurora PostgreSQL database in the second Region. Use AWS DMS to replicate the primary database to the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region.
options.D: Deploy the web tier and the application tier to a second Region. Use an Amazon Aurora global database to deploy the database in the primary Region and the second Region. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy to the second Region. Promote the secondary to primary as needed.

explanation: A is wrong: an Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions; each Region needs its own group.
B is wrong: a cross-Region replica works, but Aurora Global Database replicates faster and fails over more quickly.
C is wrong: replicating with DMS adds lag and a pipeline to run, compared with a built-in global database.
D is correct: a full stack in the second Region, Aurora Global Database with sub-second replication, and Route 53 failover give the most fault tolerance.
tldr: Multi-Region fault tolerance: a full stack in a second Region, Aurora Global Database, and Route 53 failover.

wrong_reasons.A: an Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions; each Region needs its own group.
wrong_reasons.B: a cross-Region replica works, but Aurora Global Database replicates faster and fails over more quickly.
wrong_reasons.C: replicating with DMS adds lag and a pipeline to run, compared with a built-in global database.

question: A company seeks a storage solution for its application. The solution must be highly available and scalable. The solution also must function as a file system, be mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises through native protocols, and have no minimum size requirements. The company has set up a Site-to-Site VPN for access from its on-premises network to its VPC. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
hint: Linux, NFS, elastic size, and reachable over VPN. For high availability, how many mount targets?
keywords: multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises

options.A: Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments.
options.B: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volumes.
options.C: Amazon EFS with multiple mount targets.
options.D: Amazon EFS with a single mount target and multiple access points.

explanation: A is wrong: FSx file systems are provisioned with a minimum storage size.
B is wrong: EBS Multi-Attach works only within one Availability Zone for specific instance types, and cannot be mounted from on premises.
C is correct: EFS is an elastic NFS file system with no minimum size, and a mount target in each Availability Zone keeps it highly available to instances in AWS and on premises.
D is wrong: a single mount target makes access depend on one Availability Zone.
tldr: EFS is elastic NFS for Linux with no minimum size; a mount target in each AZ keeps it highly available.

wrong_reasons.A: FSx file systems are provisioned with a minimum storage size.
wrong_reasons.B: EBS Multi-Attach works only within one Availability Zone for specific instance types, and cannot be mounted from on premises.
wrong_reasons.D: a single mount target makes access depend on one Availability Zone.

question: A company runs several AWS Lambda functions in the same AWS Region. The company notices that some calls to the Lambda functions are throttling. A business-critical function named Function A runs 100 times each second, for an average of 7 seconds. Other Lambda functions that run in the same AWS account exceed the default quota. The quota is 1,000 concurrent invocations across all functions in the same Region. A solutions architect needs to resolve the throttling issue for Function A within the account. The solutions architect must ensure that Function A meets its demands without impacting the other functions. Which combination of configurations will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
hint: Function A needs 100 x 7 = 700 concurrent executions. Reserving that leaves only 300 for everything else, so what else must change?

options.A: Set the reserved concurrency for Function A to 700.
options.B: Migrate Function A to another AWS account.
options.C: Set the provisioned concurrency for Function A to 700.
options.D: Increase the account's Lambda concurrency quota.
options.E: Migrate Lambda functions other than Function A to another AWS account.

explanation: A is correct: reserved concurrency of 700 (100 per second x 7 seconds) guarantees Function A the capacity it needs.
B is wrong: moving Function A to another account is far more work than configuration changes.
C is wrong: provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but does not guarantee capacity from the shared pool the way reserved concurrency does, and it costs more.
D is correct: reserving 700 leaves only 300 for the other functions, which already exceed the quota, so the account quota must be raised.
E is wrong: moving the other functions is a large migration, not a configuration change.
tldr: Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for a critical function; raise the account quota so other functions are not starved.

wrong_reasons.B: moving Function A to another account is far more work than configuration changes.
wrong_reasons.C: provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but does not guarantee capacity from the shared pool the way reserved concurrency does, and it costs more.
wrong_reasons.E: moving the other functions is a large migration, not a configuration change.

question: A company has a single AWS account. The company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple VPCs in one AWS Region. The company also runs workloads in an on-premises data center that connects to the company's AWS account by using AWS Direct Connect. The company needs all EC2 instances in the VPCs to resolve DNS queries for the internal example.com domain to the authoritative DNS server that is located in the on-premises data center. The solution must use private communication between the VPCs and the on-premises network. All route tables, network ACLs, and security groups are configured correctly between AWS and the on-premises data center. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
hint: Queries leave AWS through an outbound endpoint, a forwarding rule chooses which domain to send, and the rule must apply to every VPC.
keywords: authoritative DNS server that is located in the on-premises data center

options.A: Create an Amazon Route 53 inbound endpoint in all the workload VPCs.
options.B: Create an Amazon Route 53 outbound endpoint in one of the workload VPCS.
options.C: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the Forward type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.D: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the System type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.E: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with all the workload VPCs.
options.F: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the workload VPC with the new Route 53 endpoint.

explanation: A is wrong: inbound endpoints let on-premises servers query AWS DNS, which is the opposite direction.
B is correct: one outbound endpoint sends queries from AWS to the on-premises DNS server over Direct Connect.
C is correct: a Forward rule sends queries for the internal domain to the on-premises DNS server.
D is wrong: a System rule makes Resolver answer the queries itself instead of forwarding them.
E is correct: associating the rule with every workload VPC makes all instances use it, while the queries still leave through the one endpoint.
F is wrong: associating the rule only with the endpoint's VPC leaves the other VPCs unable to resolve the domain.
tldr: To resolve an on-premises domain from VPCs: Resolver outbound endpoint + Forward rule, then share or associate the rule with every VPC.

wrong_reasons.A: inbound endpoints let on-premises servers query AWS DNS, which is the opposite direction.
wrong_reasons.D: a System rule makes Resolver answer the queries itself instead of forwarding them.
wrong_reasons.F: associating the rule only with the endpoint's VPC leaves the other VPCs unable to resolve the domain.

question: A company runs production workloads in its AWS account. Multiple teams create and maintain the workloads. The company needs to be able to detect changes in resource configurations. The company needs to capture changes as configuration items without changing or modifying the existing resources. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Configuration items is AWS Config vocabulary.
keywords: without changing or modifying the existing resources

options.A: Use AWS Config. Start the configuration recorder for AWS resources to detect changes in resource configurations.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation. Initiate drift detection to capture changes in resource configurations.
options.C: Use Amazon Detective to detect, analyze, and investigate changes in resource configurations.
options.D: Use AWS Audit Manager to capture management events and global service events for resource configurations.

explanation: A is correct: the AWS Config recorder captures every configuration change as a configuration item without touching the resources.
B is wrong: drift detection only covers stacks created by CloudFormation, not resources made by hand.
C is wrong: Detective investigates security findings; it does not record configuration items.
D is wrong: Audit Manager collects evidence for audits; management events come from CloudTrail.
tldr: AWS Config records configuration items and change history for resources without modifying them.

wrong_reasons.B: drift detection only covers stacks created by CloudFormation, not resources made by hand.
wrong_reasons.C: Detective investigates security findings; it does not record configuration items.
wrong_reasons.D: Audit Manager collects evidence for audits; management events come from CloudTrail.

question: A company has several Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. These EC2 instances host applications that read and write large amounts of data to and from Amazon S3. Subnet routing currently directs all the traffic destined for the internet through a NAT gateway. The company wants to reduce the data transfer costs associated with the Amazon S3 communication. The solution must not affect the ability of the applications to communicate with Amazon S3 or the outside internet. The EC2 instances must continue to reside in a private subnet. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: S3 traffic from private subnets is going through the NAT gateway. Which free endpoint bypasses it?
keywords: large amounts of data to and from Amazon S3

options.A: Create an additional NAT gateway. Update the route table to route to the additional NAT gateway. Update the network ACL to allow Amazon S3 traffic.
options.B: Create an internet gateway. Update the route table to route traffic to the internet gateway. Update the network ACL to allow Amazon S3 traffic.
options.C: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Specify the route table to direct traffic to the gateway VPC endpoint. Attach an endpoint policy to the gateway VPC endpoint.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function outside the VPC to handle Amazon S3 requests. Attach an IAM policy to the EC2 instances that allows the EC2 instances to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation: A is wrong: another NAT gateway adds hourly and per-GB costs.
B is wrong: instances in a subnet routed to an internet gateway are no longer private, and they would need public IP addresses.
C is correct: a gateway endpoint sends S3 traffic privately at no charge, avoiding NAT processing fees, while other internet traffic still uses the NAT gateway.
D is wrong: sending S3 traffic through Lambda adds cost and complexity and does not remove data charges.
tldr: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 removes NAT gateway processing charges for S3 traffic from private subnets.

wrong_reasons.A: another NAT gateway adds hourly and per-GB costs.
wrong_reasons.B: instances in a subnet routed to an internet gateway are no longer private, and they would need public IP addresses.
wrong_reasons.D: sending S3 traffic through Lambda adds cost and complexity and does not remove data charges.

question: A company has an application that generates a large number of files. The file sizes vary between 1 KB and 10 MB. The company wants to build a store and forward solution that keeps the files in a temporary Amazon S3 location. The solution must then pre-process the files and archive the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select THREE.)
hint: Short-lived objects, many of them tiny. Watch minimum storage durations and per-object overhead in Glacier.

options.A: Configure the temporary S3 location to use the S3 Standard storage class.
options.B: Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new file is moved into the temporary S3 location.
options.C: Use event source mappings to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new file is moved into the temporary S3 location.
options.D: For files sized 128 KB or smaller, use an AWS Lambda function to add the files to a ZIP file. Offload the ZIP file to S3 Glacier when the ZIP file size reaches 1 MB.
options.E: For files sized 128 KB or smaller, use an AWS Lambda function to change the files' storage class to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA).
options.F: Configure the temporary S3 location to use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class.

explanation: A is correct: files are stored only briefly, and S3 Standard has no minimum storage duration or minimum object size charges.
B is correct: S3 Event Notifications invoke Lambda directly when a file arrives, with no extra service.
C is wrong: event source mappings are for polling sources such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not for S3.
D is correct: Glacier adds about 40 KB of overhead per object, so zipping small files into larger archives before archiving cuts cost.
E is wrong: One Zone-IA bills objects under 128 KB as 128 KB and has a 30-day minimum, which is wasteful for temporary files.
F is wrong: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum and a 128 KB minimum billable size, which are expensive for short-lived small files.
tldr: Temporary data belongs in S3 Standard (no minimum duration); bundle tiny files before archiving to cut Glacier per-object overhead.

wrong_reasons.C: event source mappings are for polling sources such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not for S3.
wrong_reasons.E: One Zone-IA bills objects under 128 KB as 128 KB and has a 30-day minimum, which is wasteful for temporary files.
wrong_reasons.F: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum and a 128 KB minimum billable size, which are expensive for short-lived small files.

question: A company is using a loosely coupled serverless architecture on AWS. The architecture consists of multiple web applications and APIs distributed across multiple teams. The company uses AWS Control Tower to provision AWS accounts. The company's development teams use AWS CloudFormation. The company wants to improve trace monitoring and gain insight into how individual services in application stacks are performing. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Tracing across services is X-Ray. Where is tracing turned on for each Lambda function and API?

options.A: Enable AWS CloudTrail across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.B: Enable AWS X-Ray across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.C: Enable Amazon CloudWatch in the CloudFormation templates.
options.D: Enable AWS X-Ray in the CloudFormation templates.

explanation: A is wrong: CloudTrail records API calls, not request traces through services.
B is wrong: X-Ray is not something Control Tower turns on for accounts; tracing is enabled on each resource.
C is wrong: CloudWatch provides metrics and logs, not end-to-end traces.
D is correct: turning on X-Ray tracing for each function and API in the CloudFormation templates traces requests through every service in the stacks.
tldr: Enable X-Ray tracing on each resource (Lambda, API Gateway) through the teams' CloudFormation templates.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudTrail records API calls, not request traces through services.
wrong_reasons.B: X-Ray is not something Control Tower turns on for accounts; tracing is enabled on each resource.
wrong_reasons.C: CloudWatch provides metrics and logs, not end-to-end traces.

question: An application uses an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance. The RDS database is becoming low on disk space. A solutions architect wants to increase the disk space without downtime. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of effort?
hint: Which RDS setting grows storage by itself when free space runs low?

options.A: Enable storage autoscaling in RDS.
options.B: Increase the RDS database instance size.
options.C: Change the RDS database instance storage type to Provisioned IOPS.
options.D: Back up the RDS database, increase the storage capacity, restore the database, and stop the previous instance.

explanation: A is correct: storage autoscaling adds storage automatically, with no downtime, whenever free space runs low.
B is wrong: a larger instance class adds CPU and memory, not disk space.
C is wrong: changing the storage type changes performance, not capacity.
D is wrong: a backup and restore is manual work and causes downtime.
tldr: RDS storage autoscaling grows storage automatically without downtime when free space runs low.

wrong_reasons.B: a larger instance class adds CPU and memory, not disk space.
wrong_reasons.C: changing the storage type changes performance, not capacity.
wrong_reasons.D: a backup and restore is manual work and causes downtime.

question: A company has multiple AWS accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations with an organizational unit (OU) for the production account and another OU for the development account. Corporate policies state that developers must use only approved AWS services in the production account. What is the MOST operationally efficient solution to control the production account?
hint: Limit which services an entire account can use, in one place.
keywords: only approved AWS services in the production account

options.A: Create a customer managed policy in IAM. Apply the policy to all users within the production account.
options.B: Create a job function policy in IAM. Apply the policy to all users within the production OU.
options.C: Create a service control policy (SCP). Apply the SCP to the production OU.
options.D: Create an IAM policy. Apply the policy in Amazon API Gateway to restrict the production account.

explanation: A is wrong: IAM policies must be attached to every user and can be changed by account administrators.
B is wrong: IAM policies are not applied to OUs.
C is correct: an SCP on the production OU limits every principal in its accounts to the approved services, managed in one place.
D is wrong: API Gateway has nothing to do with restricting AWS service usage.
tldr: SCPs on an OU cap which services every principal in its accounts can use.

wrong_reasons.A: IAM policies must be attached to every user and can be changed by account administrators.
wrong_reasons.B: IAM policies are not applied to OUs.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway has nothing to do with restricting AWS service usage.

question: A company runs an application that uses Docker containers in an on-premises data center. The application runs on a container host that stores persistent data files in a local volume. Container instances use the stored persistent data. The company wants to migrate the application to fully managed AWS services. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Fully managed containers plus shared persistent file storage without code changes.
keywords: persistent data files in a local volume

options.A: Use Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes. Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance. Mount the EBS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.B: Use Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon EFS volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.C: Use Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure the application to use the DynamoDB table for persistent storage.
options.D: Use Amazon ECS with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Create an Amazon EFS volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.

explanation: A is wrong: self-managed nodes are not fully managed, and an EBS volume is tied to one instance.
B is correct: Fargate is fully managed, and EFS gives the containers persistent file storage without code changes.
C is wrong: switching to DynamoDB means rewriting the application's file access.
