This increased demand is on read-only historical records pulled from an Amazon RDS-hosted database with custom views and queries. A solutions architect must improve performance without changing the database structure. Which approach will improve performance and MINIMIZE management overhead?
hint: Managed in-memory cache in front of RDS.

options.A: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB, move all the data, and point to DynamoDB.
options.B: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) and cache the data for the application.
options.C: Deploy Memcached on Amazon EC2 and cache the data for the application.
options.D: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) on Amazon RDS to improve cache performance.

explanation: A is wrong: moving to DynamoDB changes the database structure.
B is correct: ElastiCache for Redis is a managed cache that serves the repeated reads from memory without changing the database.
C is wrong: self-managed Memcached on EC2 adds operational work.
D is wrong: DAX works only with DynamoDB.
tldr: Managed ElastiCache (Redis) caches repeated reads in front of RDS with little operational work.

wrong_reasons.A: moving to DynamoDB changes the database structure.
wrong_reasons.C: self-managed Memcached on EC2 adds operational work.
wrong_reasons.D: DAX works only with DynamoDB.

question: A company has multiple petabytes (PB) of media files that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region. The company wants to move all the data to an S3 bucket in the us-west-2 Region as soon as possible. The company needs a data migration solution. The data needs to be verified after it is copied. The company also needs to have visibility into the data movement process. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Managed S3-to-S3 transfer with verification and reporting, in the mode built for very large datasets.
keywords: visibility into the data movement process

options.A: Use the AWS CLI to increase the max_concurrent_requests parameter value to 20 in the AWS CLI configuration. Use the AWS CLI to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.B: Use AWS DataSync with Basic mode to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.C: Use AWS DataSync with Enhanced mode to copy the data from the S3 bucket in eu-west-1 to the S3 bucket in us-west-2.
options.D: Use AWS DataSync with an agent that is deployed on an Amazon EC2 instance in eu-west-1 to move the data from the source bucket to the destination bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: the CLI gives no managed verification or progress visibility at petabyte scale.
B is wrong: Basic mode has lower performance and object-count limits for datasets this large.
C is correct: DataSync Enhanced mode copies very large S3 datasets quickly, verifies the data and reports detailed progress, with no agent.
D is wrong: no agent is needed for S3 to S3 transfers, and running one adds overhead.
tldr: DataSync Enhanced mode moves very large S3 datasets between Regions with verification, detailed metrics and higher performance.

wrong_reasons.A: the CLI gives no managed verification or progress visibility at petabyte scale.
wrong_reasons.B: Basic mode has lower performance and object-count limits for datasets this large.
wrong_reasons.D: no agent is needed for S3 to S3 transfers, and running one adds overhead.

question: A company wants to run transient workloads in an Amazon EMR cluster that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to use On-Demand Instances for core nodes and Spot Instances for task nodes. The company wants to use memory optimized EC2 instances to launch EMR clusters in the AWS Region where the company operates. The company has configured multiple subnets in multiple Availability Zones. The company must ensure that the EMR clusters are launched only in Availability Zones where specified instance types and purchasing options are available. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
hint: Which EMR configuration picks the best Availability Zone from several subnets based on capacity?
keywords: On-Demand Instances for core nodes and Spot Instances for task nodes
only in Availability Zones where specified instance types and purchasing options are available

options.A: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.B: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.
options.C: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.D: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.

explanation: A is wrong: instance groups use a single subnet and cannot choose between Availability Zones.
B is wrong: instance groups do not evaluate Availability Zone capacity.
C is correct: instance fleets across several subnets let EMR launch in an Availability Zone that has the requested instance types and purchasing options.
D is wrong: a single subnet leaves no choice of Availability Zone.
tldr: EMR instance fleets with multiple subnets let EMR choose an AZ that has the requested instance types and purchase options.

wrong_reasons.A: instance groups use a single subnet and cannot choose between Availability Zones.
wrong_reasons.B: instance groups do not evaluate Availability Zone capacity.
wrong_reasons.D: a single subnet leaves no choice of Availability Zone.

question: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances. The website processes classified data. The company stores the processed data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Because of security concerns, the company must ensure that traffic between the EC2 instances and the S3 bucket does not use public IP addresses. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Private path from EC2 to S3.
keywords: does not use public IP addresses

options.A: Create a gateway endpoint for the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 bucket policy to allow access from the endpoint.
options.B: Create an EC2 instance profile. Create an IAM policy to grant access from the EC2 instance IP addresses to the S3 bucket. Attach the IAM policy to the instance profile.
options.C: Create a NAT gateway. Update the VPC route table to route the prefixes defined by the AWS-managed S3 prefix list to the NAT gateway.
options.D: Create an IAM user that has an access key ID and a secret access key. Configure the EC2 instances to use the IAM user credentials to access the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct: a gateway endpoint keeps the traffic on private routes, and the bucket policy can limit access to that endpoint.
B is wrong: an IAM policy controls permissions, not the network path.
C is wrong: a NAT gateway still uses public IP addresses to reach S3.
D is wrong: IAM user keys do not change the network path and are insecure.
tldr: A gateway endpoint keeps EC2 to S3 traffic private; a bucket policy can limit access to that endpoint.

wrong_reasons.B: an IAM policy controls permissions, not the network path.
wrong_reasons.C: a NAT gateway still uses public IP addresses to reach S3.
wrong_reasons.D: IAM user keys do not change the network path and are insecure.

question: A company is building a new application that processes sensitive customer data. All data must comply with a data retention policy. The data must be immutable for 5 years. The data must be deleted after 10 years. The company decides to use Amazon S3 for storage and enables S3 Versioning. Which S3 configuration will meet these requirements?
hint: Truly immutable for 5 years, then deleted automatically at 10.

options.A: Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.
options.B: Configure S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a retention period of 5 years. Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.
options.C: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 10 years.
options.D: Configure S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period of 5 years. Set up S3 Lifecycle configuration rules to delete objects after 10 years.

explanation: A is wrong: lifecycle deletion alone does not make data immutable.
B is wrong: governance mode can be bypassed, so data is not truly immutable.
C is wrong: a 10-year lock keeps data immutable longer than required and does not delete it.
D is correct: compliance mode makes the data immutable for 5 years, and a lifecycle rule deletes it after 10 years.
tldr: Object Lock compliance mode for the immutable period, plus a lifecycle rule to delete at the end of retention.

wrong_reasons.A: lifecycle deletion alone does not make data immutable.
wrong_reasons.B: governance mode can be bypassed, so data is not truly immutable.
wrong_reasons.C: a 10-year lock keeps data immutable longer than required and does not delete it.

question: A company stores petabytes of historical medical information on premises. The company has a process to manage encryption of the data to comply with regulations. The company needs a cloud-based solution for data backup, recovery, and archiving. The company must retain control over the encryption key material. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Keeping control of key material means importing your own into KMS, or supplying the key yourself with each request.
keywords: retain control over the encryption key material

options.A: Create an AWS KMS key without key material. Import the company's key material into the KMS key.
options.B: Create an AWS KMS encryption key that contains key material generated by AWS KMS.
options.C: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage. Use S3 Bucket Keys with AWS KMS keys.
options.D: Store the data in an Amazon S3 Glacier storage class. Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C).
options.E: Store the data in AWS Snowball devices. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS).

explanation: A is correct: a KMS key with imported key material lets the company keep control of the material and delete it when needed.
B is wrong: key material generated by KMS is not controlled by the company.
C is wrong: Standard-IA is costlier than Glacier for archiving petabytes, and nothing here uses the company's own key material.

D is correct: S3 Glacier is the low-cost archive tier, and SSE-C means the company supplies its own key with every request; since April 2026 S3 blocks SSE-C by default on new buckets, so it must first be enabled on the bucket with PutBucketEncryption.
E is wrong: Snowball devices are for moving data, not ongoing backup and archive.
tldr: To keep control of key material: import your own material into KMS, or use SSE-C, where you supply the key with each request (SSE-C must now be enabled on the bucket first).

wrong_reasons.B: key material generated by KMS is not controlled by the company.
wrong_reasons.C: Standard-IA is costlier than Glacier for archiving petabytes, and nothing here uses the company's own key material.
wrong_reasons.E: Snowball devices are for moving data, not ongoing backup and archive.

question: A company stores data in Amazon S3. According to regulations, the data must not contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company recently discovered that S3 buckets have some objects that contain PII. The company needs to automatically detect PII in S3 buckets and to notify the company's security team. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: One service detects PII in S3; findings flow through EventBridge to a notification service.
keywords: automatically detect PII in S3 buckets

options.A: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon SNS notification to the security team.
options.B: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon SNS notification to the security team.
options.C: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData: S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon SQS notification to the security team.
options.D: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon SQS notification to the security team.

explanation: A is correct: Macie detects PII in S3, and an EventBridge rule on its sensitive-data findings sends an SNS notification to the security team.
B is wrong: GuardDuty detects threats, not PII in objects.
C is wrong: Macie is right, but SQS queues messages for programs; it does not notify people.
D is wrong: GuardDuty does not detect PII, and SQS does not notify people.
tldr: Macie detects PII in S3; route its SensitiveData findings through EventBridge to SNS to alert the team.

wrong_reasons.B: GuardDuty detects threats, not PII in objects.
wrong_reasons.C: Macie is right, but SQS queues messages for programs; it does not notify people.
wrong_reasons.D: GuardDuty does not detect PII, and SQS does not notify people.

question: A company is launching a new product and needs to collect data about the product's usage frequency. The company will review the data in an existing Amazon QuickSight dashboard. The data is in multiple formats, including Parquet, JSON, and CSV. The company wants to unify the data format and review the data by using ready-made SQL queries without using external tools. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Collect usage data into S3, convert it to one format, then query it with SQL that QuickSight can use.

options.A: Collect product data by using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Send the data to Amazon Data Firehose for processing. Set up a partition schema. Save the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.B: Set up an AWS Glue transformation job to convert data into Parquet format. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Prepare Amazon Athena queries for data reporting. Authorize connection access from the QuickSight dashboard to Athena.
options.C: Create an Amazon Managed Grafana dashboard that has prebuilt queries. Use Amazon CloudWatch as the data source. Use an Amazon EventBridge rule to run an AWS Lambda function that loads data from Amazon S3 into CloudWatch custom metrics.
options.D: Collect product information by using an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Integrate an AWS Lambda function with the REST API. Configure the Lambda function to sort data into a partition schema and store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.E: Set up an AWS Step Functions workflow to convert data into Parquet format. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct: Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose collect the usage data and store it in S3, partitioned for querying.
B is correct: a Glue job converts everything to Parquet, Athena runs saved SQL queries, and QuickSight connects to Athena.
C is wrong: Grafana and CloudWatch metrics are for monitoring, not SQL reporting on product data.
D is wrong: a custom Lambda function behind API Gateway to partition data is more work than Firehose.
E is wrong: Step Functions orchestrates steps; it does not convert data formats itself.
tldr: Kinesis and Firehose land usage data in S3; Glue converts it to Parquet; Athena queries feed QuickSight.

wrong_reasons.C: Grafana and CloudWatch metrics are for monitoring, not SQL reporting on product data.
wrong_reasons.D: a custom Lambda function behind API Gateway to partition data is more work than Firehose.
wrong_reasons.E: Step Functions orchestrates steps; it does not convert data formats itself.

question: A company manages customer data workloads across multiple AWS accounts. The company requires all Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon RDS databases, and Amazon Redshift clusters to use encryption at rest. The company must monitor compliance across accounts while reducing management effort. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: One service continuously evaluates resource settings against rules and flags noncompliant resources by itself. Which option needs no scripts and no manual review?

options.A: Use AWS Config managed rules to evaluate encryption configurations and report noncompliant resources automatically.
options.B: Use AWS Security Hub CSPM with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard. Review the security findings to identify noncompliant resources across accounts.
options.C: Create scripts that call AWS APIs to check encryption status. Run the scripts periodically on an EC2 instance.
options.D: Create scripts that call AWS APIs to check encryption status. Configure Amazon EventBridge to regularly invoke an AWS Lambda function that runs the scripts.

explanation: A is correct: AWS Config managed rules such as encrypted-volumes, rds-storage-encrypted and redshift-cluster-configuration-check evaluate each resource as it changes and report noncompliant ones automatically; an aggregator or organization conformance pack covers every account.

B is wrong: Security Hub CSPM findings would still have to be reviewed by people to pick out the encryption problems, and Security Hub itself relies on AWS Config to run its checks, so this adds a layer and a manual step.
C is wrong: custom scripts on an EC2 instance must be written, kept up to date for every resource type and account, and patched and run on a server.
D is wrong: EventBridge and Lambda remove the server, but the company still writes and maintains its own compliance scripts, which managed Config rules already provide.
tldr: Continuous compliance checks on resource settings (such as encryption at rest) = AWS Config managed rules, aggregated across accounts.

wrong_reasons.B: Security Hub CSPM findings would still have to be reviewed by people to pick out the encryption problems, and Security Hub itself relies on AWS Config to run its checks, so this adds a layer and a manual step.
wrong_reasons.C: custom scripts on an EC2 instance must be written, kept up to date for every resource type and account, and patched and run on a server.
wrong_reasons.D: EventBridge and Lambda remove the server, but the company still writes and maintains its own compliance scripts, which managed Config rules already provide.

question: A software company needs to upgrade a critical web application. The application currently runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance that the company hosts in a public subnet. The EC2 instance runs a MySQL database. The application's DNS records are published in an Amazon Route 53 zone. A solutions architect must reconfigure the application to be scalable and highly available. The solutions architect must also reduce MySQL read latency. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: An Application Load Balancer and an Auto Scaling group work inside one Region across Availability Zones. Which database option adds a reader close to the app and a standby in another AZ?

options.A: Launch a second EC2 instance in a second AWS Region. Use a Route 53 failover routing policy to redirect the traffic to the second EC2 instance.
options.B: Create and configure an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. Add the instances to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer.
options.C: Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. Create the primary DB instance and reader DB instance in separate Availability Zones.
options.D: Create and configure an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions. Add the instances to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer.
options.E: Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with cross-Region read replicas.

explanation: A is wrong: a single standby instance in another Region gives failover but no scaling, and the database would still sit on one EC2 instance.
B is correct: an Auto Scaling group across several Availability Zones behind an ALB scales the web tier and survives the loss of an AZ, and the instances can stay in private subnets.
C is correct: Aurora MySQL with a reader in a second AZ takes read traffic off the writer, lowering read latency, and Aurora promotes the reader automatically if the writer fails.
D is wrong: an Application Load Balancer and an Auto Scaling group are Regional; neither can span several Regions.
E is wrong: cross-Region read replicas help readers in other Regions, but the application runs in one Region, so they do not lower its read latency and add replication cost.
tldr: Scale the web tier with an ALB plus a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group; move MySQL to Aurora with a reader in another AZ for reads and failover.

wrong_reasons.A: a single standby instance in another Region gives failover but no scaling, and the database would still sit on one EC2 instance.
wrong_reasons.D: an Application Load Balancer and an Auto Scaling group are Regional; neither can span several Regions.
wrong_reasons.E: cross-Region read replicas help readers in other Regions, but the application runs in one Region, so they do not lower its read latency and add replication cost.

question: A trucking company is deploying an application that will track the GPS coordinates of all the company's trucks. The company needs a solution that will generate real-time statistics based on metadata lookups with high read throughput and microsecond latency. The database must be fault tolerant and must minimize operational overhead and development effort. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Microsecond reads point to an in-memory cache. Which cache plugs into one database with no changes to the application's caching logic?
keywords: high read throughput and microsecond latency
minimize operational overhead and development effort

options.A: Use Amazon DynamoDB as the database.
options.B: Use Amazon Aurora MySQL as the database.
options.C: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL as the database.
options.D: Use Amazon ElastiCache as the caching layer.
options.E: Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as the caching layer.

explanation: A is correct: DynamoDB is a serverless, Multi-AZ key-value database that handles high read throughput with no servers to manage.
B is wrong: Aurora MySQL is a relational database with millisecond reads, and it still needs instance sizing and a cache to reach microseconds.
C is wrong: RDS for MySQL has the same millisecond limit and more to manage than Aurora or DynamoDB.
D is wrong: ElastiCache can reach microseconds, but the application must be written to read from and fill the cache itself, which adds development effort.

E is correct: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that uses the same API, so the application gets microsecond reads with almost no code changes, and a DAX cluster spreads nodes across Availability Zones.
tldr: Microsecond reads on DynamoDB with little code change = DynamoDB + DAX (a write-through cache that speaks the DynamoDB API).

wrong_reasons.B: Aurora MySQL is a relational database with millisecond reads, and it still needs instance sizing and a cache to reach microseconds.
wrong_reasons.C: RDS for MySQL has the same millisecond limit and more to manage than Aurora or DynamoDB.
wrong_reasons.D: ElastiCache can reach microseconds, but the application must be written to read from and fill the cache itself, which adds development effort.

question: A company is migrating a legacy application from an on-premises data center to AWS. The application relies on hundreds of cron jobs that run between 1 and 20 minutes on different recurring schedules throughout the day. The company wants a solution to schedule and run the cron jobs on AWS with minimal refactoring. The solution must support running the cron jobs in response to an event in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Some jobs run up to 20 minutes. Which compute has no 15-minute limit, and which scheduler handles both recurring and one-time future runs?
keywords: in response to an event in the future

options.A: Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to create a recurring schedule. Run the cron job tasks as AWS Lambda functions.
options.B: Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use AWS Batch on Amazon ECS with a scheduling policy to run the cron jobs.
options.C: Create a container image for the cron jobs. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to create a recurring schedule. Run the cron job tasks on AWS Fargate.
options.D: Create a container image for the cron jobs. Create a workflow in AWS Step Functions that uses a Wait state to run the cron jobs at a specified time. Use the RunTask action to run the cron job tasks on AWS Fargate.

explanation: A is wrong: Lambda functions stop at 15 minutes, so the 20-minute cron jobs would fail.
B is wrong: AWS Batch scheduling policies set fair-share priority between jobs in a queue; they do not run jobs on a time schedule.

C is correct: EventBridge Scheduler supports cron and rate schedules as well as one-time schedules for a future date, and it can start ECS tasks on Fargate, which run the container images with no time limit and no servers.
D is wrong: a Step Functions Wait state per job would need hundreds of workflows to recreate recurring cron schedules, which is far more work than a scheduler.
tldr: Cron jobs longer than 15 minutes: EventBridge Scheduler (recurring and one-time schedules) starting ECS tasks on Fargate.

wrong_reasons.A: Lambda functions stop at 15 minutes, so the 20-minute cron jobs would fail.
wrong_reasons.B: AWS Batch scheduling policies set fair-share priority between jobs in a queue; they do not run jobs on a time schedule.
wrong_reasons.D: a Step Functions Wait state per job would need hundreds of workflows to recreate recurring cron schedules, which is far more work than a scheduler.

question: A company operates a system that requires an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic to an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances access an Amazon RDS database. The company needs to ensure that only specific resources are reachable directly from the internet. Which VPC subnet design will meet these requirements?
hint: Only the component that receives internet traffic needs a route to an internet gateway. Which tier is that?
keywords: only specific resources are reachable directly from the internet

options.A: Place the ALB, EC2 instances, and RDS database in private subnets.
options.B: Place the EC2 instances in public subnets. Place the ALB and RDS database in private subnets.
options.C: Place the ALB and EC2 instances in public subnets. Place the RDS database in private subnets.
options.D: Place the ALB in public subnets. Place the EC2 instances and RDS database in private subnets.

explanation: A is wrong: an internet-facing load balancer must sit in public subnets with a route to an internet gateway; in private subnets it cannot receive internet traffic.
B is wrong: this reverses the design: an internet-facing ALB cannot work from private subnets, and the instances would be exposed.
C is wrong: EC2 instances in public subnets can be given public IPs and become directly reachable, which the requirement rules out; the ALB already handles the internet traffic.

D is correct: the ALB is the only internet-facing component, so it goes in public subnets, while the EC2 instances and the RDS database stay in private subnets and are reached only through the ALB and the app tier.
tldr: Classic three-tier layout: internet-facing ALB in public subnets; app instances and database in private subnets.

wrong_reasons.A: an internet-facing load balancer must sit in public subnets with a route to an internet gateway; in private subnets it cannot receive internet traffic.
wrong_reasons.B: this reverses the design: an internet-facing ALB cannot work from private subnets, and the instances would be exposed.
wrong_reasons.C: EC2 instances in public subnets can be given public IPs and become directly reachable, which the requirement rules out; the ALB already handles the internet traffic.

question: A company runs a container application on a Kubernetes cluster in the company's data center. The application uses Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP) to communicate with a message queue. The data center cannot scale fast enough to meet the company's expanding business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Match each existing technology to its managed AWS equivalent: one for Kubernetes and one for AMQP.

options.A: Migrate the container application to Amazon ECS. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.
options.B: Use AWS Lambda functions to run the application. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.
options.C: Use highly available Amazon EC2 instances to run the application. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.
options.D: Migrate the container application to Amazon EKS. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.

explanation: A is wrong: moving from Kubernetes to ECS means rewriting the deployment definitions, and SQS does not support AMQP, so the messaging code would also change.
B is wrong: Lambda would need the containerized application rewritten as functions, and SQS does not support AMQP.
C is wrong: running the application directly on EC2 instances means building and running its own orchestration, which is the most overhead.

D is correct: EKS runs the existing Kubernetes workloads with a managed control plane, and Amazon MQ is a managed broker (ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ) that speaks AMQP, so neither the app nor its messaging has to change.
tldr: Kubernetes workloads → EKS; existing AMQP/MQTT/JMS messaging → Amazon MQ (SQS does not speak AMQP).

wrong_reasons.A: moving from Kubernetes to ECS means rewriting the deployment definitions, and SQS does not support AMQP, so the messaging code would also change.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda would need the containerized application rewritten as functions, and SQS does not support AMQP.
wrong_reasons.C: running the application directly on EC2 instances means building and running its own orchestration, which is the most overhead.

question: A company hosts an application on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer. The application requires a MySQL database. The database must automatically fail over to a standby instance without manual intervention. The company needs additional database capacity to support content indexing queries from a separate analytics team. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Both Multi-AZ options fail over automatically. Which one also lets other clients read from its standbys?

options.A: Create an Amazon DynamoDB database table configured with global tables.
options.B: Create an Amazon RDS database that uses Multi-AZ deployments.
options.C: Create an Amazon RDS database that uses a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment.
options.D: Create an Amazon RDS database configured with cross-Region read replicas.

explanation: A is wrong: DynamoDB is not MySQL, so the application would have to be rewritten.
B is wrong: a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has one standby that cannot serve reads, so it adds no capacity for the analytics team.
C is correct: a Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standby instances in different AZs; it fails over automatically, and the analytics team can query the reader endpoint.
D is wrong: cross-Region read replicas add read capacity but do not fail over automatically; promoting a replica is a manual step.
tldr: RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster = writer plus two readable standbys in other AZs: automatic failover and extra read capacity in one deployment.

wrong_reasons.A: DynamoDB is not MySQL, so the application would have to be rewritten.
wrong_reasons.B: a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has one standby that cannot serve reads, so it adds no capacity for the analytics team.
wrong_reasons.D: cross-Region read replicas add read capacity but do not fail over automatically; promoting a replica is a manual step.

question: A company uses multiple compute services including AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, and Amazon EC2. The company uses persistent Amazon SageMaker AI instances. The company wants to have the flexibility to scale its compute services vertically or horizontally whenever required. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Only one commitment covers Lambda, Fargate and EC2 together and still lets you change instance family, size and Region. What covers SageMaker AI instances?
keywords: AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, and Amazon EC2
scale its compute services vertically or horizontally

options.A: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the compute services. Purchase SageMaker AI Savings Plans for the SageMaker AI instances.
options.B: Purchase EC2 Savings Plans for the compute services. Purchase SageMaker AI Savings Plans for the SageMaker AI instances.
options.C: Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances for the compute services. Purchase Compute Savings Plans for the SageMaker AI instances.
options.D: Purchase Compute Savings Plans for the compute services. Purchase SageMaker AI Savings Plans for the SageMaker AI instances.

explanation: A is wrong: Reserved Instances apply only to EC2 (not Lambda or Fargate), and Standard RIs are tied to an instance family, which limits vertical scaling.
B is wrong: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply only to EC2 in one instance family and Region; they do not cover Lambda or Fargate.
C is wrong: Convertible RIs still cover only EC2, and Compute Savings Plans do not apply to SageMaker AI instances.

D is correct: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, Fargate and Lambda regardless of instance family, size or Region, so the company can scale any way it likes, and SageMaker AI Savings Plans discount the SageMaker AI instances.
tldr: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda with any family/size/Region; SageMaker AI usage needs SageMaker AI Savings Plans.

wrong_reasons.A: Reserved Instances apply only to EC2 (not Lambda or Fargate), and Standard RIs are tied to an instance family, which limits vertical scaling.
wrong_reasons.B: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply only to EC2 in one instance family and Region; they do not cover Lambda or Fargate.
wrong_reasons.C: Convertible RIs still cover only EC2, and Compute Savings Plans do not apply to SageMaker AI instances.

question: A development team is creating an event-based application that uses AWS Lambda functions. Events will be generated when files are added to an Amazon S3 bucket. The development team configures an Amazon SNS topic as the event target for the S3 bucket. Events must persist to support Lambda function scaling. The development team needs a scalable solution to process events from the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet this requirement?
hint: Events must survive until Lambda gets to them, and Lambda should scale with how many are waiting.

options.A: Create an SNS subscription that sends the events to Amazon ECS for processing before the Lambda functions process the events.
options.B: Create an SNS subscription that sends the events to Amazon EKS for processing before the Lambda functions process the events.
options.C: Create an SNS subscription that sends the events to an Amazon SQS queue. Configure the SQS queue to invoke the Lambda functions to process events.
options.D: Create an SNS subscription that sends the events to Amazon EventBridge. Configure EventBridge rules to invoke the Lambda functions to process the events.

explanation: A is wrong: Amazon ECS is not an SNS subscription target, and adding a container stage does not make the events persist.
B is wrong: Amazon EKS is not an SNS subscription target either, and it adds a cluster to run for no benefit.

C is correct: an SQS queue subscribed to the topic stores each event durably until it is processed, and the Lambda event source mapping polls the queue and scales the number of concurrent functions with the backlog.
D is wrong: EventBridge is not a standard SNS subscription target, and it invokes Lambda asynchronously without a queue that keeps events for the functions to work through.
tldr: SNS → SQS → Lambda: the queue holds events durably and Lambda polls it and scales with the backlog.

wrong_reasons.A: Amazon ECS is not an SNS subscription target, and adding a container stage does not make the events persist.
wrong_reasons.B: Amazon EKS is not an SNS subscription target either, and it adds a cluster to run for no benefit.
wrong_reasons.D: EventBridge is not a standard SNS subscription target, and it invokes Lambda asynchronously without a queue that keeps events for the functions to work through.

question: A company hosts a photo sharing web application on AWS. Users upload and share thousands of photos each hour. The company needs a durable storage solution that provides retrieval mechanisms for the photos. Most uploaded photos are not accessed often after 30 days, but the company does not want to delete older photos. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
hint: Photos are objects that are rarely read after 30 days but must stay retrievable. Which store and class lower cost without deleting anything?
keywords: does not want to delete older photos

options.A: Store the photos in an Amazon EFS file system for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) to store photos that are older than 30 days.
options.B: Store the photos in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle configurations to move photos that are older than 30 days to S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.C: Store the photos in Amazon DynamoDB for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) to store photos that are older than 30 days.
options.D: Store the photos in Amazon FSx for Lustre for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with continuous backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) to store photos that are older than 30 days.

explanation: A is wrong: EFS costs far more per GB than S3, and AWS Backup is for recovery copies, not a way to serve old photos.

B is correct: S3 is durable, cheap object storage, and a Lifecycle rule moves photos older than 30 days to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which lowers cost when access drops while keeping the photos available.
C is wrong: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so it is not built to store photos, and backups are not an access tier.
D is wrong: FSx for Lustre is high-performance scratch or HPC storage and far too expensive for a photo archive.
tldr: Photos that cool after 30 days: store them in S3 and let a Lifecycle rule move them to a cheaper class (here Intelligent-Tiering).

wrong_reasons.A: EFS costs far more per GB than S3, and AWS Backup is for recovery copies, not a way to serve old photos.
wrong_reasons.C: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so it is not built to store photos, and backups are not an access tier.
wrong_reasons.D: FSx for Lustre is high-performance scratch or HPC storage and far too expensive for a photo archive.

question: A company has thousands of developers who use Microsoft Active Directory for authentication and to manage permissions to Amazon S3 objects at scale. The company needs a solution that scales as the company grows without increasing operational overhead. The solution must give the company the ability to audit which users accessed which S3 objects. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which S3 feature maps directory users and groups straight to bucket or prefix permissions and records the end user in CloudTrail?
keywords: audit which users accessed which S3 objects

options.A: Use S3 Access Grants and AWS IAM Identity Center integrated with Active Directory users and groups.
options.B: Create S3 access points that use access point policies and IAM roles for Active Directory users.
options.C: Deploy a custom identity broker application that authenticates Active Directory users through AWS IAM Identity Center. Configure the identity broker application to use the AWS STS AssumeRole API call to provide scoped temporary credentials.
options.D: Configure AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets with resource-level S3 permissions for each Active Directory user group.

explanation: A is correct: S3 Access Grants grant S3 prefixes, buckets or objects directly to Identity Center users and groups synced from Active Directory, scale without a new IAM policy per team, and CloudTrail records the end-user identity for each access.
B is wrong: access points still need IAM roles mapped to directory users, and their policies have size limits that do not scale to thousands of developers.
C is wrong: a custom identity broker is code the company must build and run, and calls made through shared assumed roles do not tie each access back to an individual user.
D is wrong: permission sets map to IAM roles in each account, so per-group S3 resource permissions turn into many large policies, and object access is logged against the role rather than the user.
tldr: Directory users and groups → S3 data at scale with per-user auditing = S3 Access Grants with IAM Identity Center.

wrong_reasons.B: access points still need IAM roles mapped to directory users, and their policies have size limits that do not scale to thousands of developers.
wrong_reasons.C: a custom identity broker is code the company must build and run, and calls made through shared assumed roles do not tie each access back to an individual user.
wrong_reasons.D: permission sets map to IAM roles in each account, so per-group S3 resource permissions turn into many large policies, and object access is logged against the role rather than the user.

question: A company recently migrated its web application to the AWS Cloud. The company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run multiple processes to host the application. The processes include an Apache web server that serves static content. The Apache web server makes requests to a PHP application that uses a local Redis server for user sessions. The company wants to redesign the architecture to be highly available and to use AWS managed solutions. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Split the single instance into managed pieces: static files, the PHP tier, and the session store. Which option makes all three highly available?
keywords: Apache web server that serves static content
local Redis server for user sessions

options.A: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to host the static content and the PHP application. Configure Elastic Beanstalk to deploy its EC2 instance into a public subnet. Assign a public IP address.
options.B: Use AWS Lambda to host the static content and the PHP application. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to proxy requests to the Lambda function. Set the API Gateway CORS configuration to respond to the domain name. Configure Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) to handle session information.
options.C: Keep the backend code on the EC2 instance. Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster that has Multi-AZ enabled. Configure the ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster in cluster mode. Copy the frontend resources to Amazon S3. Configure the backend code to reference the EC2 instance.
options.D: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon S3 endpoint to an S3 bucket that is configured to host the static content. Configure an Application Load Balancer that targets an Amazon ECS service that runs AWS Fargate tasks for the PHP application. Configure the PHP application to use an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster that runs in multiple Availability Zones.

explanation: A is wrong: a single Elastic Beanstalk instance in a public subnet is still one point of failure, and the sessions would stay on that instance.
B is wrong: Lambda does not serve static content well and the PHP application would need to be rewritten for Lambda; CORS settings have nothing to do with availability.
C is wrong: the backend stays on a single EC2 instance, so the application is still not highly available.

D is correct: S3 behind CloudFront serves the static content, an ALB spreads requests across Fargate tasks running the PHP application, and a Multi-AZ ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster keeps sessions outside the tasks, so every tier is managed and survives the loss of an AZ.
tldr: Break up a single web server: static content on S3 + CloudFront, the app on Fargate behind an ALB, and sessions in Multi-AZ ElastiCache.

wrong_reasons.A: a single Elastic Beanstalk instance in a public subnet is still one point of failure, and the sessions would stay on that instance.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda does not serve static content well and the PHP application would need to be rewritten for Lambda; CORS settings have nothing to do with availability.
wrong_reasons.C: the backend stays on a single EC2 instance, so the application is still not highly available.

question: An ecommerce company wants a disaster recovery solution for its Amazon RDS DB instances that run Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise Edition. The company's current recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) are 24 hours. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: An RPO and RTO of 24 hours allow the cheapest DR strategy. Which option copies backups without running a second database?

options.A: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote the read replica to the primary instance.
options.B: Use AWS DMS to create RDS cross-Region replication.
options.C: Use cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.D: Copy automatic snapshots to another Region every 24 hours.

explanation: A is wrong: a cross-Region read replica runs a second SQL Server Enterprise instance all the time, which is the most expensive option and far more than a 24-hour RPO/RTO needs.
B is wrong: continuous DMS replication needs a replication instance and a target database running all the time, again far more than the requirement.
C is wrong: native backups copied with S3 replication also work, but they need native backup jobs and restore steps to set up and manage, whereas snapshot copies are built in.
D is correct: copying the automated snapshots to another Region each day meets a 24-hour RPO, a restore fits within 24 hours, and the company pays only for snapshot storage and transfer.
tldr: A 24-hour RPO/RTO only needs backup and restore: copy RDS snapshots to another Region daily and restore when needed.

wrong_reasons.A: a cross-Region read replica runs a second SQL Server Enterprise instance all the time, which is the most expensive option and far more than a 24-hour RPO/RTO needs.
wrong_reasons.B: continuous DMS replication needs a replication instance and a target database running all the time, again far more than the requirement.
wrong_reasons.C: native backups copied with S3 replication also work, but they need native backup jobs and restore steps to set up and manage, whereas snapshot copies are built in.

question: A company has multiple AWS accounts. The company needs a self-service solution to standardize infrastructure provisioning across accounts. The company's developers must be able to provision approved resources without writing infrastructure code or templates. The company's administrators must maintain governance and control access to specific configurations. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Developers must not write templates, while administrators decide what may be launched and with which settings.
keywords: without writing infrastructure code or templates

options.A: Use AWS CloudFormation with AWS Organizations to distribute templates automatically across accounts.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy templates. Configure IAM roles for cross-account access.
options.C: Use AWS Organizations with service control policies (SCPs) to manage resource provisioning across accounts.
options.D: Use AWS Service Catalog to create portfolios that contain approved products. Share portfolios across accounts.

explanation: A is wrong: CloudFormation still expects developers to work with templates, and Organizations does not distribute templates for self-service.
B is wrong: StackSets push stacks that administrators deploy centrally; they are not a self-service catalog for developers.
C is wrong: SCPs only restrict permissions; they give developers nothing to provision.

D is correct: Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved CloudFormation-based products in portfolios with constraints, share them across accounts, and developers launch them from a catalog without writing any code.
tldr: Self-service provisioning of approved resources without writing templates = AWS Service Catalog portfolios shared across accounts.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudFormation still expects developers to work with templates, and Organizations does not distribute templates for self-service.
wrong_reasons.B: StackSets push stacks that administrators deploy centrally; they are not a self-service catalog for developers.
wrong_reasons.C: SCPs only restrict permissions; they give developers nothing to provision.

question: A company is building an ecommerce application that uses a relational database to store customer data and order history. The company also needs a solution to store 100 GB of product images. The company expects the traffic flow for the application to be predictable. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Relational data goes in a relational database; images are objects. Which option puts each in its cheapest fitting store?

options.A: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL for the database. Store the product images in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.B: Use Amazon DynamoDB for the database. Store the product images in an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.C: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL for the database. Store the product images in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database.
options.D: Create three Amazon EC2 instances. Install MongoDB software on the instances to use as the database. Store the product images in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with a Multi-AZ deployment.

explanation: A is correct: RDS for MySQL fits the relational customer and order data with steady traffic, and S3 is the cheapest durable store for 100 GB of images.
B is wrong: DynamoDB is not a relational database, so the customer and order schema would have to be redesigned.
C is wrong: storing images in Aurora costs far more per GB than S3 and slows the database.
D is wrong: running MongoDB on three EC2 instances is not relational, adds management work, and storing images in a Multi-AZ RDS database is expensive.
tldr: Relational data → RDS; images and other files → S3. Never store large binaries in a database.

wrong_reasons.B: DynamoDB is not a relational database, so the customer and order schema would have to be redesigned.
wrong_reasons.C: storing images in Aurora costs far more per GB than S3 and slows the database.
wrong_reasons.D: running MongoDB on three EC2 instances is not relational, adds management work, and storing images in a Multi-AZ RDS database is expensive.

question: A company runs multiple applications across several accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company wants to be able to identify which specific workloads are driving AWS costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Accounts hold several applications each. What lets Cost Explorer split costs by workload rather than by account?
keywords: identify which specific workloads are driving AWS costs

options.A: Tag the application resources. Enable cost allocation tags in the management account. Group costs by the tag dimension in AWS Cost Explorer.
options.B: Group costs by the linked account dimension in AWS Cost Explorer.
options.C: Create an AWS Cost and Usage Report. Query the Cost and Usage Report by using Amazon Athena. Group costs by the resource ID.
options.D: Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection. Create a Linked Account type cost monitor.

explanation: A is correct: tagging resources by workload and activating those tags as cost allocation tags in the management account lets Cost Explorer group costs by workload across every account.
B is wrong: grouping by linked account shows each account's total, but each account runs several applications, so workloads cannot be told apart.
C is wrong: resource IDs show individual resources, not which workload they belong to, and building Athena queries is more work than grouping by a tag.
D is wrong: Cost Anomaly Detection alerts on unusual spending; it does not attribute costs to workloads.
tldr: Costs per workload across accounts: tag resources, activate the tags as cost allocation tags in the management account, group by tag in Cost Explorer.

wrong_reasons.B: grouping by linked account shows each account's total, but each account runs several applications, so workloads cannot be told apart.
wrong_reasons.C: resource IDs show individual resources, not which workload they belong to, and building Athena queries is more work than grouping by a tag.
wrong_reasons.D: Cost Anomaly Detection alerts on unusual spending; it does not attribute costs to workloads.

question: A company is migrating a microservices-based application to AWS. The application requires a container orchestration solution that provides high availability and automatic scaling. The company wants to reduce the operational overhead of managing the container infrastructure. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which option gives container orchestration with no servers or cluster to manage?

options.A: Deploy containers on Amazon EC2 instances. Use custom scripts to handle orchestration and scaling.
options.B: Use AWS Lambda functions to run microservices that are packaged as container images.
options.C: Use Amazon EKS to run containers and manage the cluster configuration and associated infrastructure.
options.D: Deploy containers on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type.

explanation: A is wrong: custom scripts for orchestration and scaling on EC2 are the most work and the least reliable.
B is wrong: Lambda limits run time and needs the microservices adapted to its event model, so it is not a general container orchestration platform.
C is wrong: EKS where the company manages the cluster configuration and infrastructure itself means more operational overhead than ECS on Fargate.
D is correct: ECS on Fargate is a managed orchestrator that runs tasks across Availability Zones, scales them with service auto scaling, and leaves no servers to patch or size.
tldr: Container orchestration with the least infrastructure to manage = ECS on Fargate.

wrong_reasons.A: custom scripts for orchestration and scaling on EC2 are the most work and the least reliable.
wrong_reasons.B: Lambda limits run time and needs the microservices adapted to its event model, so it is not a general container orchestration platform.
wrong_reasons.C: EKS where the company manages the cluster configuration and infrastructure itself means more operational overhead than ECS on Fargate.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The EC2 instances use a shared Amazon EFS file system to access stored code and configuration data. New application updates are pushed to the EFS file system regularly. The company needs to apply each application update as the update becomes ready. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: The new code is already on the shared EFS file system. What is the least work needed for the running instances to pick it up?
keywords: pushed to the EFS file system regularly

options.A: Configure the Auto Scaling group to tag the EC2 instances as the EC2 instances launch. Use an AWS Systems Manager Run Command to restart the application on the EC2 instances that have a specific tag.
options.B: Create a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI) for each application update. Use instance refresh to update the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group from the new AMI.
options.C: Package the application updates as patches. Schedule and apply the updates to the EC2 instances by using AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Window and Patch Manager.
options.D: Create a new launch template that uses a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to reflect the application changes. Modify the Auto Scaling group to apply the new launch template and terminate the existing EC2 instances.

explanation: A is correct: the update is already on the shared EFS file system, so the instances only need to restart the application; Run Command can target every instance with the Auto Scaling group's tag at once.
B is wrong: building a new AMI and running an instance refresh for each update replaces every instance, which is slow and unnecessary when the code lives on EFS.
C is wrong: Patch Manager applies operating system patches in maintenance windows; it is not a way to deploy application releases as soon as they are ready.
D is wrong: a new AMI and launch template for each update, then terminating instances, is the most work and causes disruption.
tldr: Code on a shared EFS file system: no new AMIs needed. Restart the app on the tagged instances with Systems Manager Run Command.

wrong_reasons.B: building a new AMI and running an instance refresh for each update replaces every instance, which is slow and unnecessary when the code lives on EFS.
wrong_reasons.C: Patch Manager applies operating system patches in maintenance windows; it is not a way to deploy application releases as soon as they are ready.
wrong_reasons.D: a new AMI and launch template for each update, then terminating instances, is the most work and causes disruption.

question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. The application needs to store and retrieve data in Amazon S3 buckets. According to regulatory requirements, the data must not travel across the public internet. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Both endpoint types keep the traffic off the internet. Compare what each one costs.
keywords: must not travel across the public internet

options.A: Deploy a NAT gateway to access the S3 buckets.
options.B: Deploy AWS Storage Gateway to access the S3 buckets.
options.C: Deploy an S3 interface endpoint to access the S3 buckets.
options.D: Deploy an S3 gateway endpoint to access the S3 buckets.

explanation: A is wrong: a NAT gateway sends traffic to S3's public endpoints and charges per hour and per GB.
B is wrong: Storage Gateway connects on-premises applications to AWS storage; it does not give EC2 instances a private path to S3.
C is wrong: an S3 interface endpoint also keeps traffic private but charges per hour per AZ and per GB.
D is correct: an S3 gateway endpoint adds a route that keeps the traffic on the AWS network and has no charge.
tldr: Private S3 access from inside a VPC at no extra cost = S3 gateway endpoint.

wrong_reasons.A: a NAT gateway sends traffic to S3's public endpoints and charges per hour and per GB.
wrong_reasons.B: Storage Gateway connects on-premises applications to AWS storage; it does not give EC2 instances a private path to S3.
wrong_reasons.C: an S3 interface endpoint also keeps traffic private but charges per hour per AZ and per GB.

question: A company is building an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application needs to handle a large number of transactions. The application requires an Amazon EBS data volume that has configurable and consistent input/output operations per second (IOPS). Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which EBS volume type lets you set IOPS and is built for steady IOPS under heavy transaction load?
keywords: configurable and consistent input/output operations per second (IOPS)

options.A: Provision EC2 instances with a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS root volume and a Cold HDD (sc1) EBS data volume.
options.B: Provision EC2 instances with a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS volume that will serve as both a root volume and a data volume.
options.C: Provision EC2 instances with a General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS root volume and a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS data volume.
options.D: Provision EC2 instances with a General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS root volume. Configure the application to store data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation: A is wrong: st1 and sc1 are throughput-oriented HDDs that cannot be boot volumes and give low IOPS.
B is wrong: st1 cannot be a boot volume and is built for large sequential throughput, not transaction IOPS.
C is correct: gp3 is a sound root volume, and io2 lets the company provision the IOPS it needs and delivers them consistently, which suits a transaction-heavy data volume.
D is wrong: S3 is object storage, not an EBS data volume with set IOPS.
tldr: Transactional data needing set, consistent IOPS = Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2); gp3 is fine for the root volume.

wrong_reasons.A: st1 and sc1 are throughput-oriented HDDs that cannot be boot volumes and give low IOPS.
wrong_reasons.B: st1 cannot be a boot volume and is built for large sequential throughput, not transaction IOPS.
wrong_reasons.D: S3 is object storage, not an EBS data volume with set IOPS.

question: A solutions architect creates a VPC that includes two public subnets and two private subnets. A corporate security mandate requires the solutions architect to launch all Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. However, when the solutions architect launches an EC2 instance that runs a web server on ports 80 and 443 in a private subnet, no external internet traffic can connect to the server. What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?
hint: A NAT gateway only lets private instances reach out. What lets internet users reach a web server in a private subnet?
keywords: launch all Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet
no external internet traffic can connect to the server

options.A: Attach the EC2 instance to an Auto Scaling group in a private subnet. Ensure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the Auto Scaling group identifier.
options.B: Provision an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a public subnet. Add the EC2 instance to the target group that is associated with the ALB. Ensure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the ALB.
options.C: Launch a NAT gateway in a private subnet. Update the route table for the private subnets to add a default route to the NAT gateway. Attach a public Elastic IP address to the NAT gateway.
options.D: Ensure that the security group that is attached to the EC2 instance allows HTTP traffic on port 80 and HTTPS traffic on port 443. Ensure that the DNS record for the website resolves to the public IP address of the EC2 instance.

explanation: A is wrong: an Auto Scaling group has no address that DNS can resolve to, and the instances would still be unreachable from a private subnet.
B is correct: an internet-facing ALB in a public subnet receives the internet traffic and forwards it to the private instance as a target, so the server stays in a private subnet.
C is wrong: a NAT gateway only allows connections that the instances start, and it must sit in a public subnet; it never accepts inbound connections.
D is wrong: an instance in a private subnet has no public IP address or internet route, so security group rules alone do not make it reachable.
tldr: Inbound web traffic to private instances: an internet-facing ALB in public subnets with the instances as targets.

wrong_reasons.A: an Auto Scaling group has no address that DNS can resolve to, and the instances would still be unreachable from a private subnet.
wrong_reasons.C: a NAT gateway only allows connections that the instances start, and it must sit in a public subnet; it never accepts inbound connections.
wrong_reasons.D: an instance in a private subnet has no public IP address or internet route, so security group rules alone do not make it reachable.

question: A company has an Amazon S3 data lake. The company needs a solution that transforms the data from the data lake and loads the data into a data warehouse every day. The data warehouse must have massively parallel processing (MPP) capabilities. Data analysts then need to create and train machine learning (ML) models by using SQL commands on the data. The solution must use serverless AWS services wherever possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Which warehouse is MPP and has a serverless option, and which ETL service is serverless? Then which one trains models with SQL?
keywords: machine learning (ML) models by using SQL commands

options.A: Run a daily Amazon EMR job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Redshift. Use Amazon Redshift ML to create and train the ML models.
options.B: Run a daily Amazon EMR job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Aurora Serverless. Use Amazon Aurora ML to create and train the ML models.
options.C: Run a daily AWS Glue job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Redshift Serverless. Use Amazon Redshift ML to create and train the ML models.
options.D: Run a daily AWS Glue job to transform the data and load the data into Amazon Athena tables. Use Amazon Athena ML to create and train the ML models.

explanation: A is wrong: Redshift and Redshift ML fit, but EMR clusters are not serverless, so the solution does not use serverless services wherever possible.
B is wrong: Aurora Serverless is a relational database, not an MPP data warehouse, and Aurora ML calls models that already exist; it does not create and train them with SQL.
C is correct: Glue runs serverless ETL jobs, Redshift Serverless is a serverless MPP data warehouse, and Redshift ML creates and trains models with CREATE MODEL SQL statements.
D is wrong: Athena queries data in place and is not a data warehouse that data is loaded into, and there is no Athena ML feature for training models.
tldr: Serverless ETL into a serverless MPP warehouse with SQL-based ML = Glue → Redshift Serverless → Redshift ML.

wrong_reasons.A: Redshift and Redshift ML fit, but EMR clusters are not serverless, so the solution does not use serverless services wherever possible.
wrong_reasons.B: Aurora Serverless is a relational database, not an MPP data warehouse, and Aurora ML calls models that already exist; it does not create and train them with SQL.
wrong_reasons.D: Athena queries data in place and is not a data warehouse that data is loaded into, and there is no Athena ML feature for training models.

question: A company has a large data workload that runs for 6 hours each day. The company cannot lose any data while the process is running. A solutions architect is designing an Amazon EMR cluster configuration to support this critical data workload. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Core nodes store HDFS data; task nodes only compute. Which nodes can be interrupted safely, and does the cluster need to run all day?

options.A: Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.B: Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.C: Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance and the core nodes and task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.D: Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance, the core nodes on Spot Instances, and the task nodes on Spot Instances.

explanation: A is wrong: the node layout is safe, but a long-running cluster pays for 18 idle hours every day.

B is correct: a transient cluster runs only for the 6-hour job, On-Demand primary and core nodes protect the cluster and its HDFS data, and Spot task nodes add cheap capacity that can be interrupted without losing data.
C is wrong: core nodes store HDFS data, so running them on Spot risks losing data when instances are reclaimed.
D is wrong: Spot core nodes risk data loss, and a long-running cluster pays for idle time.
tldr: EMR: primary and core nodes On-Demand (they hold state and data), task nodes on Spot; use a transient cluster for a job of a few hours a day.

wrong_reasons.A: the node layout is safe, but a long-running cluster pays for 18 idle hours every day.
wrong_reasons.C: core nodes store HDFS data, so running them on Spot risks losing data when instances are reclaimed.
wrong_reasons.D: Spot core nodes risk data loss, and a long-running cluster pays for idle time.

question: A startup company has a social media application that produces large volumes of incoming write requests on the company's Amazon DynamoDB tables. The company wants to respond to unpredictable surges in table usage in the shortest possible time. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: The surges cannot be predicted, and any scaling that reacts after the fact leaves a gap.
keywords: large volumes of incoming write requests

options.A: Use DynamoDB with provisioned capacity mode.
options.B: Use DynamoDB auto scaling.
options.C: Use DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options.D: Use DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode.

explanation: A is wrong: provisioned capacity without scaling throttles requests once a surge goes above the set capacity.
B is wrong: auto scaling adjusts provisioned capacity over minutes using CloudWatch alarms, so sudden surges are throttled before it catches up.
C is wrong: DAX caches reads; it does nothing for a surge in write requests.
D is correct: on-demand mode serves requests as they arrive and adapts to the traffic level at once, so surges are handled without capacity planning or scaling delays.
tldr: Unpredictable, spiky DynamoDB traffic = on-demand capacity mode; it serves surges without capacity planning.

wrong_reasons.A: provisioned capacity without scaling throttles requests once a surge goes above the set capacity.
wrong_reasons.B: auto scaling adjusts provisioned capacity over minutes using CloudWatch alarms, so sudden surges are throttled before it catches up.
wrong_reasons.C: DAX caches reads; it does nothing for a surge in write requests.

question: A company has a critical ecommerce application that uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a Multi-AZ deployment. The company's analytics team has increased the number of queries it uses to generate reports. The increase in usage has resulted in application performance degradation. The analytics team requires near real-time data consistency in its reports. The analytics team must be able to generate reports even if the DB instance is offline. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: The Multi-AZ standby cannot serve queries. Which option gives the analysts a separate, near real-time copy they can read?
keywords: even if the DB instance is offline

options.A: Take a snapshot and restore the snapshot as a separate DB instance to run the queries.
options.B: Modify the DB instance to use a larger instance size.
options.C: Direct the queries to the standby DB instance endpoint.
options.D: Add a read replica. Direct the queries to the read replica endpoint.

explanation: A is wrong: a restored snapshot is only as current as the snapshot, so the reports would not be near real-time.
B is wrong: a larger instance still serves both workloads from one database and does not help when that instance is offline.
C is wrong: the standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot be read; it exists only for failover.
D is correct: a read replica is updated asynchronously within seconds, takes the report queries off the primary, and is a separate instance the analysts can still query if the primary is offline.
tldr: Move reporting off the primary with an RDS read replica: near real-time asynchronous copy, separate endpoint, survives a primary outage.

wrong_reasons.A: a restored snapshot is only as current as the snapshot, so the reports would not be near real-time.
wrong_reasons.B: a larger instance still serves both workloads from one database and does not help when that instance is offline.
wrong_reasons.C: the standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot be read; it exists only for failover.

question: A company uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL database and read replicas to host video catalog data. Mobile applications query the read replicas to access the video catalog data. The RDS for MySQL database uses stored procedures for catalog and licensing logic. During peak hours, mobile application users experience delayed video catalog updates because of replica synchronization lag. The company needs to eliminate synchronization delays and preserve stored procedure compatibility. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: RDS MySQL replicas replay the binary log, so they can fall behind. Which MySQL-compatible engine has replicas that read the same storage as the writer?

options.A: Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Replace the read replicas with Aurora Replicas. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling. Maintain the stored procedures in Aurora MySQL.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster in front of the database. Modify the mobile applications to query the cache before accessing the database. Replace the stored procedures with AWS Lambda functions.
options.C: Migrate the database to a MySQL database that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Use compute optimized EC2 instances for all replica nodes. Maintain the stored procedures on the EC2 instances.
options.D: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Provision read capacity units to support the required throughput. Configure on-demand capacity scaling. Replace the stored procedures with DynamoDB streams and AWS Lambda functions.

explanation: A is correct: Aurora Replicas read the same shared cluster volume as the writer instead of replaying a binary log, so replica lag is typically far below a second; Aurora MySQL runs the existing stored procedures, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas at peak.
B is wrong: a cache in front of the database adds its own staleness, and rewriting the stored procedures as Lambda functions and changing the mobile apps is a lot of work.
C is wrong: self-managed MySQL on EC2 still uses binary log replication with the same lag, and adds patching and failover work.
D is wrong: DynamoDB has no stored procedures, so the catalog and licensing logic would have to be rebuilt, which is the opposite of preserving compatibility.
tldr: Replica lag on RDS MySQL: move to Aurora MySQL, whose replicas share the cluster storage (lag usually well under a second) and keep MySQL features.

wrong_reasons.B: a cache in front of the database adds its own staleness, and rewriting the stored procedures as Lambda functions and changing the mobile apps is a lot of work.
wrong_reasons.C: self-managed MySQL on EC2 still uses binary log replication with the same lag, and adds patching and failover work.
wrong_reasons.D: DynamoDB has no stored procedures, so the catalog and licensing logic would have to be rebuilt, which is the opposite of preserving compatibility.

question: A company runs an application by using microservices on Amazon EKS. The application processes HTTP API requests that must be distributed to specific services based on the request path. The company requires a solution that minimizes operational overhead and infrastructure costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?
hint: Routing on the URL path is a layer 7 feature. Which load balancer does it, and how does EKS create one for you?
keywords: minimizes operational overhead and infrastructure costs

options.A: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision a Network Load Balancer.
options.B: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision an Application Load Balancer.
options.C: Use an AWS Lambda function to route the requests to Amazon EKS.
options.D: Use Amazon API Gateway to route the requests to Amazon EKS.

explanation: A is wrong: a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route by HTTP request path.
B is correct: the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an ALB from Kubernetes Ingress resources, and the ALB routes each request to the right service by its path, with no extra components to run.
C is wrong: a Lambda function as a router is custom code that adds latency, cost and maintenance.
D is wrong: API Gateway in front of EKS also needs a VPC link and a load balancer, so it adds cost and parts when an ALB alone can route by path.
tldr: Path-based routing to EKS services = AWS Load Balancer Controller provisioning an ALB from Kubernetes Ingress resources.

wrong_reasons.A: a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route by HTTP request path.
wrong_reasons.C: a Lambda function as a router is custom code that adds latency, cost and maintenance.
wrong_reasons.D: API Gateway in front of EKS also needs a VPC link and a load balancer, so it adds cost and parts when an ALB alone can route by path.

question: A company is building an application that needs to process real-time streaming data. The application must process and transform the data and then store the data for later analysis. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Which options are all serverless, and which one ingests streaming data in order?

options.A: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest streaming data. Configure Amazon EC2 instances to process and transform data records from the data streams. Configure the EC2 instances to store the processed and transformed data in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database.
options.B: Send streaming data to an Amazon SQS queue. Configure AWS Lambda functions to process the data in the SQS queue. Store the processed data in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.C: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest streaming data. Configure an AWS Lambda function to process and transform data records from the data streams. Configure the Lambda function to store the processed and transformed data in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.D: Send streaming data to an Amazon SNS topic. Create an application to process the data on an Amazon EC2 instance. Store the processed data in an Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cache.

explanation: A is wrong: EC2 instances for processing and an RDS database add servers to scale and patch.
B is wrong: SQS is a message queue rather than a streaming service: it does not keep records in order for several consumers or allow replay, and this option has no real stream to ingest from.
C is correct: Kinesis Data Streams ingests the stream, a Lambda event source mapping reads batches from the shards and transforms them, and DynamoDB stores the results, all with no servers to manage.
D is wrong: an application on EC2 needs to be built and run, and Memcached is an in-memory cache with no durability, so it cannot store data for later analysis.
